question: What is the primary purpose of nursing research?

options.A: To increase the cost of hospital equipment
options.B: To replace clinical judgment with rigid rules
options.C: To give doctors more administrative duties
options.D: To expand knowledge and improve patient care

explanation: Research is fundamentally about discovering new information that directly enhances how nurses care for their patients. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why should nursing care rely on research instead of just doing things 'the way we've always done it'?

options.A: Hospital managers forbid nurses from using traditional methods
options.B: Habits always cost more money to maintain
options.C: Habits are often based on outdated assumptions rather than proof
options.D: Traditions change too quickly for nurses to keep track

explanation: Exactly! Relying only on old habits can lead to poor patient care because traditions often lack scientific proof. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h1)

question: When scientific research is described as 'empirical', what does that mean?

options.A: It is based on direct observation and real-world data
options.B: It focuses only on historical events from the past
options.C: It changes every time a new person reads the report
options.D: It relies entirely on the personal opinion of the researcher

explanation: Well done! Empirical simply means it is built on tangible evidence and real-world observations, not just guesses. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why is it important for other researchers to be able to repeat (replicate) a study?

options.A: It ensures the original researchers make a lot of money
options.B: It proves the findings are dependable if others get similar results
options.C: It allows the hospital to fire extra nursing staff
options.D: It guarantees that no human errors ever occurred

explanation: Spot on! When different people follow the same steps and get similar results, we can trust the findings much more. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h2)

question: In a research study, what do we call the 'independent variable'?

options.A: The total number of patients who refused to participate
options.B: The intervention or cause manipulated by the researcher
options.C: The final outcome measured at the end of the project
options.D: The random error that occurs during data collection

explanation: You got it! The independent variable is the active ingredient or change that the researcher introduces to see what happens. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h3)

question: A nurse studies if walking 30 minutes daily lowers blood pressure in adults. What is the dependent variable here?

options.A: Blood pressure level
options.B: The time of day
options.C: The adult participants
options.D: Walking 30 minutes daily

explanation: Great job! The dependent variable is the outcome you are measuring—in this case, the blood pressure responding to the walk. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h3)

question: How would you simply define a 'nursing theory'?

options.A: A strict set of disciplinary rules for student nurses
options.B: A proven drug recipe used in emergency rooms
options.C: An organized set of concepts explaining a phenomenon
options.D: A list of hospital equipment costs for the year

explanation: Correct! A theory gives us a helpful framework to explain why things happen and guides our nursing actions. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h4)

question: How do theory and research work together in nursing?

options.A: Theory replaces the need for any actual patient research
options.B: Research tests theories in practice, and practice helps shape new theories
options.C: Research only happens when there are no theories available
options.D: Theories are only used by doctors while nurses do research

explanation: Exactly! They go hand-in-hand: research tests our ideas in real life, and those findings help refine our theories. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the main focus of qualitative research?

options.A: Exact numerical measurements and statistics
options.B: Calculating hospital budgets and supply costs
options.C: Laboratory experiments involving chemical compounds
options.D: Human experiences, words, and meanings

explanation: Spot on! Qualitative research looks at the rich stories, feelings, and experiences of people rather than just numbers. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why is applied research so helpful in everyday clinical nursing?

options.A: It relies entirely on mathematical formulas instead of patients
options.B: It aims to solve immediate, practical patient care problems
options.C: It never requires ethical approval from an institutional board
options.D: It costs nothing to conduct in a busy hospital ward

explanation: You nailed it! Applied research tackles the real, everyday challenges we face right there at the bedside. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h5)

question: What does 'evidence-based practice' mean for a working nurse?

options.A: Doing whatever the patient demands regardless of safety
options.B: Relying solely on intuition during emergencies
options.C: Using current best research evidence alongside clinical expertise
options.D: Following hospital traditions without questioning them

explanation: Great choice! EBP blends solid research, your clinical judgment, and what matters to the patient to give the best care. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a benefit of research in nursing?

options.A: Improving patient outcomes through proven interventions
options.B: Helping reduce ineffective and wasteful clinical procedures
options.C: Eliminating the need for nurses to ever think critically
options.D: Building a unique scientific foundation for the profession

explanation: That's right! Research actually requires MORE critical thinking, as we must thoughtfully apply evidence rather than replacing our brains. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T1#GNS217_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing inquiry?

options.A: To systematically search for knowledge relevant to practice
options.B: To write hospital policies without clinical input
options.C: To punish nurses who make clinical mistakes
options.D: To reduce the number of hospital admissions

explanation: Nursing inquiry is all about finding reliable knowledge to improve how we care for patients, teach, and run hospitals. You'll see this come up often in practice! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why shouldn't nurses always rely purely on tradition and routine when answering clinical questions?

options.A: Patients refuse to be treated with older methods
options.B: Traditional practices are always illegal to perform
options.C: Routine methods may be outdated and lack evidence
options.D: Hospital management strictly forbids traditional habits

explanation: We've all heard "we've always done it this way!" But checking newer evidence helps us give the safest, best care possible. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which pattern of knowing represents the science of nursing derived from research?

options.A: Empirical knowing
options.B: Ethical knowing
options.C: Aesthetic knowing
options.D: Personal knowing

explanation: Empirical knowing is your go-to science foundation—it relies on objective, observable data and actual research findings. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h2)

question: A nurse uses self-awareness to connect authentically with a frightened patient. Which pattern of knowing is this?

options.A: Personal knowing
options.B: Empirical knowing
options.C: Aesthetic knowing
options.D: Ethical knowing

explanation: Personal knowing is about looking inward and using self-reflection to build a genuine, trusting relationship with your patient. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is a major downside of relying only on authority figures for your clinical decisions?

options.A: Institutional leaders have no clinical background
options.B: Authority figures are impossible to locate in a hospital
options.C: Senior nurses refuse to speak with junior staff
options.D: Experts may base views on custom rather than evidence

explanation: Even experienced experts can fall back on outdated habits if their views aren't backed by solid, current research. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h3)

question: A junior nurse is told to do a dressing change a certain way simply because 'that is how we've always done it here.' What type of inquiry is this?

options.A: Traditional and authority-based inquiry
options.B: Randomized controlled testing
options.C: Empirical scientific inquiry
options.D: Systematic qualitative inquiry

explanation: Relying on past custom and instructions from senior staff without checking the literature is traditional and authority-based inquiry. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the main goal of using controls in the scientific method?

options.A: To make the research study take longer to finish
options.B: To ensure only senior doctors can read the study
options.C: To prevent patients from asking questions
options.D: To minimize bias and error in the results

explanation: Controls help make sure our findings reflect reality instead of outside accidental factors messing up the data. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h4)

question: A researcher wants to see if a new handwashing technique cuts down ward infections better than the old one. What is the best approach?

options.A: Guessing the outcome based on personal feelings
options.B: Asking the oldest nurse on the ward for advice
options.C: Following whatever tradition feels most comfortable
options.D: The scientific method using a structured trial

explanation: Testing a clear idea with structured observation is the true hallmark of the scientific method in action. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h4)

question: What type of data is primarily collected in quantitative research?

options.A: Numbers and statistical measurements
options.B: Open-ended audio interviews
options.C: Artistic drawings of patient feelings
options.D: Detailed personal life stories

explanation: Think 'QUANtitative = QUANTITY.' It's all about numbers, measurements, and stats! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which research question is best suited for a quantitative approach?

options.A: What are the emotional challenges of being a first-time ward manager?
options.B: How do patients describe their spiritual journey in palliative care?
options.C: What does it feel like to live with chronic kidney failure?
options.D: Does a 10mg dose of medication lower blood pressure faster than a 5mg dose?

explanation: Because we are measuring dosage amounts and blood pressure numbers, we need a numerical, quantitative study design. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the main focus of qualitative research in healthcare?

options.A: Calculating exact drug dosages for safe administration
options.B: Measuring blood pressure and laboratory values
options.C: Counting the number of patient bed days
options.D: Exploring human experiences and meanings

explanation: Think 'QUALItative = QUALITY or descriptions.' It seeks to understand the subjective experiences and stories of individuals. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why would a nurse researcher choose a qualitative design over a quantitative one?

options.A: To calculate the exact statistical cost of hospital equipment
options.B: To measure the physical growth rate of pediatric patients
options.C: To understand the deep personal meaning of living with a chronic illness
options.D: To prove which medication cures a bacterial infection fastest

explanation: Qualitative research shines when we want to capture human emotion, personal perspectives, and lived experiences through words. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h6)

question: What does a mixed methods research study combine?

options.A: Hospital budgets and staffing rosters
options.B: Traditional habits and modern myths
options.C: Physician opinions and nursing guesses
options.D: Quantitative and qualitative approaches

explanation: You guessed it—mixed methods brings together both numerical data and narrative stories into one study! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why is mixed methods inquiry so useful in complex healthcare settings?

options.A: It is the cheapest and fastest method to complete
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any statistical tests
options.C: It prevents patients from participating in interviews
options.D: It captures both measurable outcomes and human experiences

explanation: Combining hard numbers with human stories gives researchers a much fuller, richer picture of complicated health problems. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is required before a human participant can take part in a research study?

options.A: A signed agreement to work on the ward
options.B: Voluntary informed consent
options.C: Approval from hospital accountants
options.D: Payment of a research fee

explanation: Ethics first! Participants must fully understand what the study involves and willingly agree to join without any pressure. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h8)

question: Which of the following groups needs special protective measures during research studies?

options.A: Healthy adult nurses working day shifts on the ward
options.B: Vulnerable populations such as children and unconscious patients
options.C: Senior medical doctors leading research teams
options.D: Hospital administrators reviewing the annual budget

explanation: Vulnerable groups need extra safeguards because they might not be fully able to give true voluntary consent on their own. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T2#GNS217_U1_T2_h8)

question: Why do nursing students need to learn about different sources of knowledge?

options.A: To eliminate the need for clinical experience entirely
options.B: To memorize every historical medical text ever written
options.C: To understand why clinical guidelines change and why evidence matters
options.D: To learn how to diagnose patients without a doctor

explanation: Knowing where knowledge comes from helps you see why nursing care changes for the better as new evidence comes to light. You've got this! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h1)

question: How do subjective ways of knowing (like personal feelings) differ from structured ways of knowing?

options.A: Subjective ways are guaranteed to be 100 percent accurate
options.B: Structured ways are only used by doctors, never by nurses
options.C: Structured ways cannot be used in a hospital setting
options.D: Subjective ways rely more on personal feelings and habits rather than testing

explanation: Subjective knowing is often based on gut feeling or tradition. Structured methods, on the other hand, use careful testing to prove what works. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h1)

question: When healthcare workers rely on 'tradition,' what is their main mindset?

options.A: Only randomized controlled trials can guide nursing care
options.B: We do it this way because we have always done it this way
options.C: Personal gut feelings are more reliable than textbooks
options.D: Every patient requires a completely unique laboratory workup

explanation: Tradition leans heavily on past habits and routines rather than checking if newer, better methods are available. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main danger of relying only on tradition in nursing care?

options.A: It increases the financial cost of basic hospital linens
options.B: It causes nursing schools to close down unexpectedly
options.C: It makes doctors refuse to work with nursing staff
options.D: It can keep nurses doing things that are outdated or harmful

explanation: When we only follow old routines without questioning them, unsafe or outdated practices can stick around much longer than they should. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h2)

question: In the 'method of authority,' why do people accept a piece of information as true?

options.A: The patient insists that the treatment works
options.B: The information comes from a respected or credible source
options.C: The data was gathered through personal dreams
options.D: The procedure takes less than five minutes to complete

explanation: This method relies on trust in someone perceived as an expert, like a senior consultant or an established textbook. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h3)

question: When is relying on an 'authority figure' most risky in clinical practice?

options.A: When the nurse is washing their hands before a procedure
options.B: When the textbook was published in the current year
options.C: When the hospital policy was written yesterday by a committee
options.D: When the authority figure speaks outside their specific field or is biased

explanation: Even brilliant experts can be wrong when talking about topics outside their actual specialty! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h3)

question: How does knowledge happen when using intuition?

options.A: By reading old medical journals in the hospital library
options.B: Through strict adherence to hospital procedure manuals
options.C: By performing a double-blind randomized clinical trial
options.D: Through an immediate gut feeling or hunch without conscious reasoning

explanation: Intuition skips the slow steps of logic and gives you a sudden inner sense that something is right (or wrong). [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why should nurses be careful about relying solely on intuition for patient care?

options.A: It always leads to incorrect clinical decisions
options.B: It is subjective, hard to explain, and prone to personal bias
options.C: It only works for surgical nurses and never for public health nurses
options.D: It is illegal to document gut feelings on a patient chart

explanation: Gut feelings can give you a helpful warning, but they need to be backed up by real, measurable patient assessments. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the core idea behind deductive reasoning?

options.A: Trusting a senior doctor purely because of their title
options.B: Moving from a general premise down to a specific conclusion
options.C: Accepting traditional habits without asking any questions
options.D: Gathering random facts until a pattern appears by chance

explanation: Deduction takes a known general rule and applies it to a specific situation to figure out what follows. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is the biggest weakness of using the rational (logical) method by itself?

options.A: It cannot be written down on paper or spoken aloud
options.B: It ignores all forms of mathematical calculation
options.C: A flawed starting premise leads to an incorrect conclusion
options.D: It takes too many years to complete a single calculation

explanation: Logic is only as good as its starting point. If your first assumption is wrong, your final answer will be wrong too! [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h5)

question: How do you acquire knowledge through the empirical method?

options.A: Through direct observation and sensory experience
options.B: Through pure logical thought without looking at the patient
options.C: By accepting traditional beliefs without testing
options.D: By waiting for a sudden gut feeling or intuition

explanation: Empiricism means gathering facts using your own senses—like looking at a wound, touching a pulse, or listening to lung sounds. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h6)

question: A nurse uses a stethoscope to listen to bowel sounds after surgery. Which method of acquiring knowledge is this?

options.A: Rational method
options.B: Method of tenacity
options.C: Empirical method
options.D: Method of authority

explanation: Listening with a stethoscope is a direct sensory observation, which is the exact definition of the empirical method. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h6)

question: What two main ingredients are combined in the scientific method?

options.A: Tradition and personal intuition
options.B: Gut feelings and unverified habits
options.C: Rational logic and empirical observation
options.D: Strict authority and superstition

explanation: Science brings together logical thinking and real, measurable sensory data to test ideas properly. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why is 'replication' (repeating a study) so important in scientific nursing research?

options.A: It proves that the researcher is more important than the clinician
options.B: It helps verify whether original results were accurate and reliable
options.C: It eliminates the need for patient consent in clinical trials
options.D: It ensures that hospital policies never change again

explanation: When different researchers repeat a study and get the same results, we can trust that the findings are solid and dependable. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h7)

question: Besides published research, what else does evidence-based nursing practice bring together?

options.A: Superstition and historical habits
options.B: Personal intuition and strict tradition
options.C: Clinical expertise and patient preferences
options.D: Hospital budgets and physician seniority

explanation: Good evidence-based practice blends the best research with your own clinical judgment and what matters most to the patient. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h8)

question: What should you do when a patient's unique situation doesn't quite match standard textbook research?

options.A: Assume the research is completely useless and rely only on guesses
options.B: Use critical thinking to balance the evidence with the patient's individual reality
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately without further assessment
options.D: Ignore the patient's symptoms because the textbook study is always right

explanation: Research gives us a great roadmap, but every patient is unique. As a nurse, you use your critical thinking to adapt care to the person in front of you. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T3#GNS217_U1_T3_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of classifying research studies?

options.A: To organize studies by characteristics for easy evaluation
options.B: To make all research papers the exact same length
options.C: To eliminate the need for statistical data analysis
options.D: To ensure that every study uses qualitative methods

explanation: Categorizing studies helps nurses quickly understand study designs and evaluate evidence quality for clinical use. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is research classification valuable in evidence-based nursing practice?

options.A: It proves that quantitative research is superior to qualitative work
options.B: It helps identify the strength of evidence for clinical decisions
options.C: It guarantees that patient outcomes will always improve instantly
options.D: It removes the requirement for ethical approval in local clinics

explanation: Different classifications indicate different levels of evidence reliability, which guides safe and effective patient care. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h1)

question: Applied research differs from basic research because applied research aims to...

options.A: solve practical, real-world problems directly
options.B: expand general knowledge without clinical use
options.C: avoid collecting data from human subjects
options.D: eliminate the need for literature reviews

explanation: Applied research specifically targets immediate, practical issues like improving patient care protocols. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h2)

question: A nurse studies the daily fluid intake habits of pregnant women in a rural clinic without changing their routine. What type of research is this?

options.A: Descriptive research
options.B: Interventional research
options.C: Experimental research
options.D: Basic laboratory research

explanation: Descriptive research observes and documents existing characteristics without manipulating any variables. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h2)

question: What type of data is primarily collected in qualitative research?

options.A: Exact dosage measurements
options.B: Words and narratives
options.C: Numerical statistics
options.D: Laboratory blood counts

explanation: Qualitative research focuses on gathering words, experiences, and meanings rather than numbers. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h3)

question: A researcher uses both numerical surveys and detailed interviews to study patient satisfaction in a ward. This approach is called...

options.A: purely basic research
options.B: mixed methods research
options.C: exclusively qualitative research
options.D: strictly descriptive research

explanation: Combining both numerical data and narrative interviews constitutes a mixed methods study design. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h3)

question: A study that collects data from patients at one single point in time is known as...

options.A: a cross-sectional study
options.B: a prospective study
options.C: a longitudinal study
options.D: a retrospective study

explanation: Cross-sectional studies capture a single snapshot of data without following subjects over time. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why would a researcher choose a longitudinal study design over a cross-sectional one?

options.A: To eliminate all possibilities of participant drop-out
options.B: To avoid dealing with human participants altogether
options.C: To finish data collection within a single afternoon
options.D: To observe changes and outcomes over an extended period

explanation: Longitudinal studies track the same subjects over time, allowing researchers to see how variables change or develop. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h4)

question: Where does field research typically take place?

options.A: Inside a highly controlled laboratory
options.B: In natural, real-world settings
options.C: Only within pharmaceutical manufacturing plants
options.D: Exclusively inside computer simulation software

explanation: Field research is conducted in natural environments like community clinics or patient homes rather than labs. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is a major advantage of conducting research in a controlled laboratory environment?

options.A: Zero need for ethical clearance
options.B: Direct replication of messy home environments
options.C: High control over extraneous variables
options.D: Guaranteed participation from random patients

explanation: Laboratories allow researchers to isolate variables and minimize outside interference. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h5)

question: An experimental nursing study differs from a non-experimental study because the experimental study includes...

options.A: exclusively historical medical records
options.B: only qualitative interview transcripts
options.C: an active intervention by the researcher
options.D: no human participants at any stage

explanation: Experimental designs involve introducing an intervention or treatment to measure its effect on outcomes. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which scenario describes a non-experimental nursing study?

options.A: Testing whether a new antiseptic reduces surgical site infections
options.B: Comparing two distinct surgical incision closure techniques
options.C: Administering a trial drug to lower hypertensive crisis rates
options.D: Assessing burnout levels among nurses in accident and emergency

explanation: Observing and measuring existing burnout without introducing an intervention is non-experimental. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h6)

question: How does understanding research classification help a bedside nurse?

options.A: It replaces the hospital protocol handbook entirely
options.B: It removes the need to read professional nursing journals
options.C: It helps evaluate if study findings apply to local patients
options.D: It allows nurses to perform major surgeries independently

explanation: Knowing study classifications helps nurses determine if research evidence fits their specific clinical environment and patient demographic. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h7)

question: The critical appraisal of research literature directly supports which core nursing concept?

options.A: Evidence-based practice
options.B: Hospital budget allocation
options.C: Pharmaceutical manufacturing
options.D: Biomedical equipment repair

explanation: Evaluating research quality and design is the cornerstone of implementing evidence-based practice in nursing. [learn more](GNS217_U1_T4#GNS217_U1_T4_h7)

question: As student nurses, why do we bother learning and doing nursing research?

options.A: To build an evidence base for safe patient care
options.B: To replace traditional bedside nursing duties entirely
options.C: To prove that old hospital policies are useless
options.D: To complicate simple clinical procedures

explanation: You got this! Research gives us solid proof and reliable facts so we can take care of our patients safely and with confidence. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h1)

question: How is formal nursing research different from just guessing or solving a ward problem on the spot?

options.A: Research follows a structured and disciplined pathway
options.B: Research never involves human participants
options.C: Research is always performed by doctors alone
options.D: Casual problem-solving uses more statistics

explanation: Spot on! While we solve ward problems every day, formal research follows careful, step-by-step rules to make sure the answers are truly reliable. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h1)

question: When a study is called 'empirical,' what kind of information is the researcher using?

options.A: Ancient cultural traditions and habits
options.B: Personal opinions and unproven gut feelings
options.C: Strictly theoretical guesses without testing
options.D: Observable and measurable real-world data

explanation: Well done! Empirical just means 'I can see it, touch it, or measure it in the real world'—not just guessing or going with a gut feeling. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h2)

question: Why must a research project always be done in a systematic, step-by-step way?

options.A: To prevent the researcher from talking to patients
options.B: To make the final written report look very long
options.C: To ensure steps happen in a logical, orderly sequence
options.D: To make data analysis completely unnecessary

explanation: Exactly! Being systematic keeps everything organized and orderly so that anyone reading your study can follow what you did. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h2)

question: If a research study is 'verifiable,' what does that mean for other nurses?

options.A: The study can only be performed once in history
options.B: Only the original author is allowed to read the data
options.C: Other researchers can replicate it and get similar results
options.D: The results change every time a new nurse looks at them

explanation: You got it! Verifiable means another nurse or researcher can repeat your steps and find the same results, proving it's trustworthy. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h3)

question: Why is using good, clear logic so important from the beginning to the end of your research?

options.A: It guarantees the hospital will fund the research project
options.B: It ensures conclusions directly match the gathered evidence
options.C: It removes the need for any statistical calculations
options.D: It stops patients from withdrawing from the study

explanation: Spot on! Sound logic stops us from making wild claims that our actual data doesn't back up. Keep it logical! [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the main reason a researcher tries to control variables in a study?

options.A: To ensure patients never experience any side effects
options.B: To make the research process as fast as possible
options.C: To isolate the specific effect of the intervention being tested
options.D: To hide unwanted data from the final report

explanation: Brilliant! Controlling variables helps you say for sure: 'Yes, this specific drug or nursing action is what made the patient better.' [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h4)

question: Imagine a nurse is testing a new handwashing technique and makes sure every ward uses the exact same water temperature and soap brand. Why do this?

options.A: To punish wards that do not follow hospital rules
options.B: To prove that water temperature is the only cause of illness
options.C: To control outside variables that could affect infection rates
options.D: To save money on purchasing hospital cleaning supplies

explanation: Exactly right! By keeping things like water and soap the same, you make sure any change in infection rates is truly because of the new technique, not random outside factors. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why do we say that research is a 'cyclical' process?

options.A: Studies always return to their starting point without changing
options.B: The data collection phase lasts for exactly twelve months
options.C: Researchers must repeat the exact same study every single year
options.D: Completed studies naturally spark new questions and further research

explanation: You got it! Research is like a wheel that keeps turning—answering one question always leads to fresh, exciting new mysteries to solve. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h5)

question: What happens when a nursing study uncovers surprising or unexpected findings?

options.A: The entire scientific community must stop investigating that topic
options.B: The study is immediately thrown away and hidden
options.C: Patients on the ward are taken off their medication
options.D: It opens the door for new research questions and follow-up studies

explanation: Spot on! Unexpected results are not failures; they challenge what we think we know and kick off the next round of helpful research. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h5)

question: What does it mean for a nursing research project to show 'originality'?

options.A: Adding fresh insights or applying concepts in a new setting
options.B: Inventing a brand-new hospital building design
options.C: Writing a research paper without using any past references
options.D: Copying successful studies from foreign countries word-for-word

explanation: Well done! Originality means bringing a fresh perspective, new data, or trying an existing idea in a brand-new setting like our local Nigerian hospitals. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is a study that just repeats common knowledge without any new angle considered weak?

options.A: It will automatically cause patients to experience adverse events
options.B: It requires too much expensive laboratory equipment
options.C: It is illegal under international medical guidelines
options.D: It fails to advance the existing body of professional knowledge

explanation: Correct! As nursing students, we want our studies to push the profession forward, not just restate things everyone already knows. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the golden rule of ethics when doing research with human beings?

options.A: Ensuring participants pay for taking part in the study
options.B: Keeping the true purpose of the study a secret forever
options.C: Publishing the real names of every patient in the local newspaper
options.D: Protecting participants from harm and respecting their autonomy

explanation: You nailed it! Patient safety, voluntary choice, and dignity always come first—before any research data. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why must a nurse researcher be extra careful when asking their own hospital patients to join a study?

options.A: Patients always know more about research than the nurses do
options.B: Patients might feel pressured to agree out of fear of poor care
options.C: Patients are legally barred from signing consent forms
options.D: Hospital management forbids nurses from talking to patients

explanation: Spot on! Patients might feel too scared to say 'no' because they worry it might affect the medical care they get from the ward. We must always make participation 100% voluntary! [learn more](GNS217_U2_T1#GNS217_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why do we bother doing nursing research in the first place?

options.A: To increase hospital funding through grants
options.B: To replace traditional nursing duties with laboratory tasks
options.C: To bridge the gap between clinical theory and bedside practice
options.D: To reduce the number of nursing staff needed on wards

explanation: Spot on! Research isn't just for textbooks; it directly helps us connect what we learn in class to giving better, safer care to our patients at the bedside. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h1)

question: As a nurse, why should you carefully review published research before using it?

options.A: To decide if findings are safe and appropriate to apply to patients
options.B: To find grammatical errors in academic writing
options.C: To publish their own papers in foreign journals
options.D: To prove that researchers always make mistakes

explanation: You've got this! Checking research helps you figure out what is actually safe and helpful to bring into your daily ward routine. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it tricky to study things like pain and fatigue in patients?

options.A: They only occur in male patients
options.B: They are abstract and hard to define uniformly
options.C: They never change over the course of an illness
options.D: They cannot be recorded on any medical chart

explanation: Exactly! Pain and fatigue look and feel different to every single person, which makes them harder to measure the same way every time. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h2)

question: What happens if a researcher doesn't clearly define an abstract idea like anxiety in their study?

options.A: The study becomes completely free of bias
options.B: The hospital automatically receives more research funding
options.C: Study results become hard to compare across different populations
options.D: Patients stop feeling anxious during procedures

explanation: Spot on! If everyone defines a term differently, it's impossible to fairly compare the results or repeat the study elsewhere. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the 'Hawthorne effect' in a research study?

options.A: The sudden drop in blood pressure caused by new drugs
options.B: Alteration of behavior by subjects who know they are being observed
options.C: A permanent loss of study participants over time
options.D: The financial cost of running a large hospital trial

explanation: Correct! People naturally change how they act when they know someone is watching them, which can sometimes trick our research findings. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h3)

question: A researcher notices many patients stopped attending a 6-month weight loss study before it ended. What is this called?

options.A: The Hawthorne effect
options.B: A confounding variable
options.C: Attrition bias
options.D: Random assignment

explanation: You nailed it! 'Attrition' just means people dropping out over time, which can leave us with a lopsided group of results. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h3)

question: What usually causes recall bias when patients fill out questionnaires?

options.A: Researchers losing patient charts in the archive
options.B: Faulty electrical wiring in hospital monitors
options.C: Doctors prescribing the wrong medication doses
options.D: Patients forgetting past events or giving socially desirable answers

explanation: Spot on! Human memory is tricky, and sometimes patients tell us what they think we want to hear rather than what actually happened. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is it important to regularly calibrate hospital research equipment?

options.A: To prevent measurement errors that ruin data accuracy
options.B: To shorten the time required for patient interviews
options.C: To make the equipment look newer to inspectors
options.D: To ensure patients pay lower hospital bills

explanation: Exactly right! If our tools aren't accurate, our data won't be either. Calibration keeps our numbers honest. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h4)

question: Who must give consent if a research study involves confused elderly patients?

options.A: Legally authorized representatives
options.B: The head hospital security guard
options.C: Any nurse working on the shift
options.D: The pharmaceutical company sponsor

explanation: Well done! When patients can't speak for themselves, we rely on their trusted representatives to protect their rights and safety. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the main job of an Institutional Review Board (IRB)?

options.A: To collect financial taxes from hospital laboratories
options.B: To market new medical products to the public
options.C: To protect the rights and safety of human research subjects
options.D: To write nursing textbooks for universities

explanation: Spot on! The IRB acts as a safety shield, making sure no research harms participants or takes advantage of them. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a common daily challenge for clinical nurses who want to get involved in research?

options.A: Being forced to write books instead of working
options.B: Balancing heavy patient care duties with data collection tasks
options.C: Having too much free time during morning shifts
options.D: Lacking access to any patients in the hospital

explanation: You got it! Ward work is busy, and finding extra time to gather data on top of caring for patients is no small feat. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h6)

question: How do tight budgets usually affect a clinical research study?

options.A: They automatically improve the accuracy of patient records
options.B: They limit sample sizes and shorten follow-up periods
options.C: They make patients more willing to take experimental drugs
options.D: They eliminate the need for ethical board review

explanation: Exactly! Without enough funding, researchers simply cannot afford to track as many people or follow them for very long. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the big advantage of running a small pilot study first?

options.A: It helps identify design flaws before a large-scale trial
options.B: It guarantees that the main study will cost no money
options.C: It proves the research hypothesis is 100 percent true
options.D: It replaces the need for an institutional review board

explanation: Spot on! A pilot study is like a dress rehearsal; it lets us fix mistakes before spending big money on the main event. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why should researchers be honest about study limitations in their published papers?

options.A: To trick reviewers into approving weak methodologies
options.B: To avoid paying taxes on research grants
options.C: To make the paper shorter and easier to read
options.D: To ensure readers interpret findings with appropriate caution

explanation: You nailed it! Total honesty about what a study *couldn't* do stops clinicians from misapplying the results on the wards. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T2#GNS217_U2_T2_h7)

question: What major historical event drove Florence Nightingale to collect and analyze health data?

options.A: The American Civil War
options.B: The Crimean War
options.C: World War I
options.D: The 1918 Influenza Pandemic

explanation: Nightingale systematically tracked illness and death rates among wounded soldiers during her service in the Crimean War to prove the value of hospital sanitation. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why did Florence Nightingale use visual diagrams like her famous polar area chart?

options.A: To hide negative hospital statistics from military generals
options.B: To predict future disease outbreaks in European cities
options.C: To make complex data easy for non-medical leaders to understand
options.D: To decorate official reports for the royal family

explanation: Visual charts helped politicians and military commanders quickly grasp the shocking death toll caused by poor hygiene rather than battle wounds. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h1)

question: What was the main focus of nursing studies during the early part of the twentieth century?

options.A: Hospital staffing and nursing education
options.B: Molecular genetics and cellular biology
options.C: Pharmacological drug trials
options.D: Advanced surgical techniques

explanation: Early research mostly looked at how to organize nursing schools, manage hospital routines, and assign student workloads efficiently. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h2)

question: Why did clinical research take a backseat to educational studies in early nursing history?

options.A: Nursing was heavily focused on following fixed hospital routines and administrative tasks
options.B: Physicians refused to let nurses learn how to read write research papers
options.C: There were no sick patients available in hospitals for students to study
options.D: Government laws strictly forbade nurses from observing patient symptoms

explanation: Great job thinking this through! Back then, nursing was driven more by strict hospital traditions and routines than by independent science, so administrative duties came first. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h2)

question: What development after World War II greatly boosted the progress of nursing research?

options.A: The creation of graduate master's programs in nursing
options.B: The invention of the electronic medical record
options.C: The complete replacement of doctors by nurse practitioners
options.D: The banning of all traditional hospital routines

explanation: Master's programs gave nurses the formal scientific training required to design, fund, and conduct independent research studies. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h3)

question: A nurse researcher in the 1950s would most likely study which of these topics?

options.A: Surgical techniques for performing open-heart bypass
options.B: The genetic mapping of rare hereditary blood disorders
options.C: The biochemical structure of synthetic antibiotic molecules
options.D: Methods to improve patient comfort and manage post-operative pain

explanation: You got this! After WWII, nursing science shifted its focus directly to bedside care issues, like helping patients heal comfortably and managing their symptoms. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h3)

question: What was a major focus of nursing research during the 1970s and 1980s?

options.A: Eliminating the need for clinical bedside nurses
options.B: Studying hospital kitchen sanitation procedures
options.C: Designing hospital computer software systems
options.D: Developing distinct nursing theories and models

explanation: Nurses during this era worked hard to create their own theoretical frameworks rather than relying solely on medical or psychological models. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why did nurse leaders in the 1970s feel the need to build their own unique nursing theories?

options.A: To replace all medical textbooks with nursing journals
options.B: To prove that nurses were more important than physicians in hospitals
options.C: To better explain and guide the unique aspects of professional nursing care
options.D: To satisfy strict government tax requirements for universities

explanation: Think of it this way: borrowed theories couldn't fully capture what makes nursing special. Leaders needed original frameworks to truly guide everyday clinical practice. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h4)

question: What does Evidence-Based Practice primarily combine in clinical decision-making?

options.A: Research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient preferences
options.B: Pharmaceutical advertisements and medical textbook theory
options.C: Traditional habits, personal opinions, and trial-and-error
options.D: Hospital budget reports, doctor orders, and insurance rules

explanation: True evidence-based practice brings together solid research findings, the nurse's professional experience, and the values of the patient. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a part of Evidence-Based Practice?

options.A: Respecting the unique values and choices of patients
options.B: Following strict historical traditions without question
options.C: Using clinical expertise to guide nursing actions
options.D: Critically appraising current research studies

explanation: Spot on! Evidence-based practice encourages us to question 'we've always done it this way' and instead rely on solid science and critical thinking. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is a major focus of nursing research in settings like Nigeria today?

options.A: Designing private space rockets for healthcare workers
options.B: Reducing maternal mortality and improving community health
options.C: Testing luxury spa treatments for hospital patients
options.D: Replacing all clinical nurses with computer robots

explanation: Spot on! Local nursing research here at home focuses on solving pressing local issues, especially keeping mothers and children healthy in our communities. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h6)

question: A modern nurse researcher studying how telehealth apps improve blood pressure control in rural communities is demonstrating which current trend?

options.A: Abandoning clinical practice for pure laboratory biology
options.B: Integrating technology into nursing care solutions
options.C: Returning to early twentieth-century hospital routines
options.D: Relying exclusively on 19th-century sanitary data

explanation: Modern nursing science actively investigates digital health tools like telehealth to extend quality care to remote populations. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T3#GNS217_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing research?

options.A: To reduce the number of working hours for staff
options.B: To develop trustworthy knowledge for the profession
options.C: To replace doctors in making medical diagnoses
options.D: To eliminate the need for clinical experience

explanation: Spot on! Nursing research is all about building a solid foundation of proven facts to make patient care better across the board. You've got this! [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is relying purely on old habits and trial-and-error risky in nursing?

options.A: It is usually too expensive for the hospital to fund
options.B: It takes too much paperwork to document
options.C: It can compromise patient safety and clinical outcomes
options.D: It prevents nurses from working in private clinics

explanation: Exactly! Doing things just because 'we've always done it that way' can sometimes hurt patients. We always want our care backed by solid evidence. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h1)

question: Who laid the early foundation for nursing research by collecting data on hospital sanitation in the 19th century?

options.A: Linda Richards
options.B: Clara Barton
options.C: Mary Seacole
options.D: Florence Nightingale

explanation: Well done! Florence Nightingale used numbers and stats during the Crimean War to prove that clean environments save lives. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h2)

question: In the early days following Nightingale's work, what was the main focus of nursing studies?

options.A: Advanced surgical interventions
options.B: Pharmaceutical drug development
options.C: Hospital financial management
options.D: Nursing education and training methods

explanation: Spot on! Before diving heavily into clinical care, early nurse researchers first wanted to figure out the best ways to train and educate nurses. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h2)

question: What are the three core elements that make up Evidence-Based Practice (EBP)?

options.A: Financial cost, administrative goals, and staff availability
options.B: Hospital policy, doctor orders, and nursing intuition
options.C: Research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values
options.D: Textbook theory, peer pressure, and trial-and-error

explanation: Brilliant! EBP is a sweet spot that combines what science proves, what your clinical skills tell you, and what the patient actually prefers. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h3)

question: How does research directly help you practice evidence-based care on the ward?

options.A: It dictates the exact salary scale for nursing staff
options.B: It eliminates all documentation requirements for nurses
options.C: It replaces the need to assess individual patient preferences
options.D: It provides tested proof of which clinical interventions work best

explanation: Correct! Research gives us the reliable facts we need to update our daily ward procedures and get better results for our patients. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is a direct benefit of using research-backed repositioning schedules on the ward?

options.A: An increase in daily patient discharge rates
options.B: A reduction in hospital-acquired pressure ulcers
options.C: Fewer mandatory shifts for junior nurses
options.D: Lower hospital electricity and utility bills

explanation: You got it! Studies on skin care clearly show that turning patients on a structured schedule keeps their skin safe and prevents painful bedsores. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h4)

question: A nurse wants to lower catheter-related infections in the surgical ward. Following research principles, what should be done first?

options.A: Stop using catheters entirely for every single surgical patient
options.B: Review current research for evidence-based catheter care guidelines
options.C: Wait for patient complaints before changing the cleaning routine
options.D: Punish staff members who report high infection numbers

explanation: Spot on! Whenever we want to solve a clinical problem, checking current research helps us find safe, proven protocols that actually work. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h4)

question: How does nursing research help hospital managers and policymakers?

options.A: By providing data to support safe staffing ratios and health laws
options.B: By helping hospitals avoid paying taxes on medical supplies
options.C: By ensuring that doctors have total control over hospital budgets
options.D: By removing the need for government health ministries

explanation: Correct! Research gives leaders the hard numbers and proof they need to make smart laws and build safer healthcare systems. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why are administrative decisions much better when they are backed by nursing research?

options.A: It guarantees that the hospital will never face any lawsuits
options.B: It balances financial costs with patient safety and staff efficiency
options.C: It reduces the salaries of senior nursing management
options.D: It allows administrators to ignore staff complaints completely

explanation: Well done! Research helps managers make smart financial choices while still keeping patients safe and nurses supported. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h5)

question: What does publishing nursing research primarily help the profession establish?

options.A: Total control over all medical school curricula
options.B: A unique and independent body of knowledge
options.C: The right to practice medicine without a license
options.D: Exemption from hospital ethical oversight boards

explanation: Spot on! Having our own distinct set of scientific knowledge is what truly makes nursing a respected, independent profession. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h6)

question: How does engaging in research impact a nurse's daily confidence and independence in practice?

options.A: It empowers nurses to make independent, evidence-backed care decisions
options.B: It restricts nurses to performing only basic hygiene tasks
options.C: It forces nurses to ask doctors for permission before speaking
options.D: It stops nurses from collaborating with other health workers

explanation: Exactly! When you know the 'why' behind your care from research, you walk onto the ward with real professional confidence. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is it important to conduct nursing research right here in Nigeria instead of relying only on foreign studies?

options.A: Local challenges like resource limits and culture differ from other regions
options.B: Foreign research studies are always fake and poorly written
options.C: Nigerian hospitals are not allowed to read international journals
options.D: International research never deals with patient care issues

explanation: You got it! Solutions have to fit our local Nigerian environment, culture, and available resources to actually work on our wards. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h7)

question: A Nigerian nurse wants to help reduce maternal mortality in a rural community. What is the best first step?

options.A: Tell the villagers to stop using traditional birth attendants without offering alternatives
options.B: Wait for international organizations to solve the problem without local data
options.C: Import expensive foreign medical equipment that the local clinic cannot power
options.D: Conduct a local study to identify specific barriers preventing women from seeking antenatal care

explanation: Spot on! Local research helps us uncover the real root causes of a problem so we can design solutions that truly fit the community. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is a very common challenge that stops clinical nurses from using research on busy shifts?

options.A: Lack of time during busy hospital shifts
options.B: An excess of research journals in the breakroom
options.C: Mandatory daily research exams for all staff
options.D: Too much free time available on the ward

explanation: True! Heavy workloads and packed hospital shifts mean nurses often struggle to find free time to sit down and read research papers. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h8)

question: How can hospital management best help nurses overcome barriers to using research?

options.A: Requiring every nurse to publish a textbook before promotion
options.B: Providing access to journal databases and encouraging ward journal clubs
options.C: Punishing nurses who ask questions about traditional ward routines
options.D: Banning all clinical discussions during the morning handover shift

explanation: Brilliant! Creating an encouraging learning environment with easy resource access makes research feel friendly and doable for the whole team. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T4#GNS217_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of nursing research?

options.A: To lower the financial cost of operating public hospitals
options.B: To reduce the number of working hours for hospital staff
options.C: To develop knowledge for nursing practice and improve patient outcomes
options.D: To replace physicians in diagnosing complex medical conditions

explanation: Nursing research focuses on building a scientific base for nursing care so patients receive the safest and most effective interventions. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is local health research important for nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: Foreign textbooks are too expensive for local nursing students to buy
options.B: International organizations pay large grants exclusively to clinical nurses
options.C: Nigerian hospitals require every nurse to publish a paper before promotion
options.D: Western guidelines do not address specific local health challenges and cultural realities

explanation: You've got this! Local research matters because health issues like malaria management and maternal care need solutions tailored to our environment, rather than just copying foreign data. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h1)

question: What is a common research duty for a bedside staff nurse?

options.A: Collecting data and identifying study participants
options.B: Funding major multi-center clinical drug trials
options.C: Writing national health policy legislation
options.D: Publishing textbooks for medical schools

explanation: Bedside nurses are closest to patients, making them well-suited to spot eligible participants and gather accurate clinical data. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h2)

question: What is the main job of a Nurse Principal Investigator?

options.A: Distributing meal trays to study participants in the clinic
options.B: Cleaning and sterilizing surgical instruments after research surgeries
options.C: Designing studies, securing funding, and overseeing ethical implementation
options.D: Administering daily bed baths to patients on the surgical ward

explanation: Think of a Principal Investigator as the captain of the study—they plan the project, find financial support, and make sure everything follows ethical guidelines. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h2)

question: What are the three main pillars that make up evidence-based practice?

options.A: Patient age, family background, and disease diagnosis
options.B: Research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values
options.C: Hospital policy, physician orders, and insurance budgets
options.D: Textbook theory, nursing tradition, and administrative rules

explanation: EBP is a balanced approach that requires combining valid research findings with the nurse's professional judgment and what matters to the patient. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h3)

question: A nurse wants to know if a new wound dressing heals ulcers faster. What is her very first step?

options.A: Ask a clear, focused clinical question about the two dressings
options.B: Write a formal research paper for an international journal
options.C: Ask the hospital management to buy the new dressing brand
options.D: Change the dressing on all patients in the ward immediately

explanation: Great clinical thinking starts by asking the right question! Before searching or applying evidence, you must first define what you are trying to find out. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of an Institutional Review Board (IRB) in research?

options.A: To provide financial grants and equipment to student researchers
options.B: To grade the academic performance of nursing postgraduate students
options.C: To market the finished research paper to private pharmaceutical companies
options.D: To protect the rights, safety, and well-being of human research subjects

explanation: An ethics committee or IRB reviews study proposals beforehand to make sure human participants will not be harmed or exploited. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which option best describes true informed consent in clinical research?

options.A: An agreement signed by the hospital manager on behalf of the patients
options.B: A verbal promise made by the researcher that no complications will occur
options.C: An ongoing, voluntary dialogue ensuring participants understand risks and rights
options.D: A quick signature obtained by a doctor right before a surgical procedure

explanation: Informed consent isn't just a one-time signature. It's a continuous conversation making sure the participant is fully aware and knows they can walk away anytime. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which of these is a major barrier to nursing research in busy hospitals?

options.A: Excessive amounts of free time during shifts
options.B: Too many available financial grants and computers
options.C: Heavy clinical workloads and staffing shortages
options.D: Strict bans on publishing local healthcare data

explanation: Spot on! When nurse-to-patient ratios are high and everyone is exhausted, it's really tough to find the energy or time for research. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why does a lack of mentorship often slow down research growth for young nurses?

options.A: Mentorship is illegal in most public Nigerian teaching hospitals
options.B: Experienced nurses prefer to keep research findings a secret
options.C: Experienced mentors charge expensive fees to teach data analysis
options.D: Young nurses miss out on guidance, confidence building, and practical support

explanation: Having a senior colleague to show you the ropes makes all the difference. Without guidance, new researchers often feel overwhelmed and give up. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the main goal of a nursing journal club in a hospital?

options.A: To raise money for the hospital's annual end-of-year party
options.B: To review and discuss recent research articles in a supportive setting
options.C: To punish nurses who make medication errors on the ward
options.D: To sell textbooks and medical equipment to patients

explanation: Journal clubs are fun and supportive! They help nurses build confidence in reading and discussing research papers together. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which of the following does NOT help build a strong research culture?

options.A: Discouraging nurses from reading studies done by other healthcare professions
options.B: Creating mentorship programs between senior and junior staff
options.C: Establishing local grants to fund small nursing projects
options.D: Providing protected time during work hours for research activities

explanation: Healthcare is team-based! Shutting out studies from other professions hurts teamwork and slows down evidence-based practice. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the main goal of nursing research?

options.A: To increase the financial revenue of private health institutions
options.B: To replace traditional medical diagnoses with nursing diagnoses
options.C: To build a knowledge base that guides practice and improves patient outcomes
options.D: To reduce the administrative workload of hospital managers

explanation: Spot on! Nursing research is all about finding out what works best so we can give our patients the safest, highest quality care possible. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why can relying only on 'the way we've always done it' (clinical tradition) be tricky in healthcare?

options.A: It prevents nurses from communicating effectively with doctors
options.B: It causes immediate legal action against the hospital management
options.C: It automatically increases the cost of purchasing hospital equipment
options.D: It can keep outdated habits alive that no longer serve the patient well

explanation: Great job! Just because we've 'always done it that way' doesn't mean it's still the best way. Science and care methods keep improving for our patients' benefit. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is a major everyday hurdle for bedside nurses who want to do research?

options.A: Heavy clinical workloads and shift duties
options.B: The absence of any medical terminology in nursing
options.C: Mandatory laws forbidding nurses from collecting data
options.D: A complete lack of patients in government hospitals

explanation: Too true! Juggling busy ward shifts and direct patient care leaves very little breathing room for extra projects. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why can a lack of training in data analysis make nurses shy away from research?

options.A: It makes interpreting study findings and writing reports feel overwhelming
options.B: It stops patients from answering interview questions honestly
options.C: It automatically disqualifies the nurse from holding a practicing license
options.D: It prevents the hospital from buying medical supplies

explanation: It's completely normal to feel intimidated by data at first. Without a little guidance, crunching numbers and writing reports can feel like a heavy mountain to climb. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h2)

question: When there's no institutional funding for a nursing study, what do nurses often end up doing?

options.A: Abandon clinical duties to work in foreign labs
options.B: Rely entirely on free pharmaceutical samples
options.C: Close down the hospital ward permanently
options.D: Sponsor their own studies out of pocket

explanation: That's right! Many passionate nurses use their own money to cover things like printing and transport just to get important studies done. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h3)

question: How do poor internet and lack of journal access affect local nursing research?

options.A: They prevent nurses from wearing their uniforms to work
options.B: They force patients to travel abroad for medical treatments
options.C: They increase the number of medication errors in the wards
options.D: They make thorough literature reviews and data analysis very difficult

explanation: Spot on. Without good internet access, checking what other researchers around the world have discovered becomes a massive struggle. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why do we consider hospitalized patients a 'vulnerable group' when doing research?

options.A: They automatically agree with every instruction a doctor gives
options.B: They may feel forced to join a study because they rely on the hospital for care
options.C: They do not have any legal rights while admitted as patients
options.D: They are physically unable to speak or write down their thoughts

explanation: Exactly. Because patients depend on us for healing, they might worry that saying 'no' to a study will change how we treat them. We must always protect their freedom to choose! [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is true about getting valid informed consent from a patient?

options.A: It is only necessary if the research involves major surgical procedures
options.B: It transfers the ownership of the patient's medical records to the researcher
options.C: It involves clear communication and genuine voluntary agreement, not just a signature
options.D: It can be waived by the nurse if the patient looks too tired to read

explanation: You got it! Consent isn't just about ticking a box or signing a paper—it's an ongoing conversation where the patient truly understands and freely agrees to take part. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why do we really need home-grown, local nursing research data in Nigeria?

options.A: Strict penalties for hospitals that do not run clinical trials
options.B: Government regulations forcing every nurse to publish a book
options.C: The desire of international pharmaceutical companies to sell drugs
options.D: The need for evidence that reflects regional and cultural realities

explanation: Brilliant! Textbook solutions from abroad don't always fit our local environment. We need research that speaks directly to our specific communities and resources. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h5)

question: A nurse notices pressure sores are common in the elderly ward and tries a new turning schedule. What is this an example of?

options.A: An illegal medical experiment on vulnerable human subjects
options.B: A quality improvement project based on clinical observation
options.C: A violation of hospital administrative policy
options.D: A financial investment in medical equipment manufacturing

explanation: Spot on! Noticing a ward problem and trying a practical nursing fix to make things better is a classic quality improvement project. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is a major benefit of a junior nurse being mentored by an experienced researcher?

options.A: It allows the junior nurse to escape night shift duties permanently
options.B: It provides mentorship that demystifies publication and data analysis
options.C: It fulfills the legal requirement for hospital budget approval
options.D: It guarantees immediate international grants for the hospital

explanation: Mentorship is a game-changer! Having an experienced guide takes the fear out of research and shows you that publishing is totally doable. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why should nursing schools include hands-on mini-projects during training?

options.A: It provides free labor for hospital administrative departments
options.B: It stops students from pursuing bedside clinical nursing careers
options.C: It builds confidence and practical skills in carrying out future studies
options.D: It ensures students pass their board exams without studying textbooks

explanation: Exactly! Doing small projects early on takes away the anxiety so you feel like a capable researcher long before you graduate. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T6#GNS217_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of nursing research?

options.A: To eliminate the need for patient preferences
options.B: To develop trustworthy evidence for nursing practice
options.C: To increase the cost of hospital operations
options.D: To replace clinical judgment with rigid rules

explanation: Nursing research systematically gathers facts to guide safe and effective care choices. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is relying solely on clinical tradition dangerous in modern healthcare?

options.A: Patients always reject care based on historical habits
options.B: Traditions are often outdated and unsupported by current evidence
options.C: Traditions cost too much money to maintain in hospitals
options.D: Physicians refuse to follow traditional nursing methods

explanation: Habits passed down through generations of staff may be ineffective or even harmful compared to modern tested methods. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the very first step in conceptualizing a research study?

options.A: Discharging patients who fit the study criteria
options.B: Identifying a specific clinical problem or topic
options.C: Submitting the final paper to a medical journal
options.D: Purchasing expensive data analysis software

explanation: A researcher must first pinpoint what issue needs investigating before taking any further steps. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why must a researcher conduct a literature review early in the process?

options.A: To decide which nurses will be punished for mistakes
options.B: To see what is already known and avoid repeating past work
options.C: To find patients willing to participate in the study
options.D: To determine the exact financial cost of the hospital

explanation: Reading prior studies prevents wasting time on questions that have already been answered thoroughly. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h2)

question: What does a quantitative research design primarily rely on?

options.A: Long personal diaries and emotional stories
options.B: Historical paintings and cultural myths
options.C: Numerical data and statistical analysis
options.D: Unstructured casual conversations

explanation: Quantitative studies focus on measurements, counts, and statistical tests to evaluate variables. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h3)

question: A nurse researcher wants to understand how patients feel emotionally while recovering from open-heart surgery. Which design is most appropriate?

options.A: Qualitative design
options.B: Laboratory chemical analysis
options.C: Quantitative experimental design
options.D: Financial audit design

explanation: Qualitative designs excel at capturing deep human experiences, feelings, and personal perspectives. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is a sample in a research study?

options.A: A small subset of people chosen to represent a larger population
options.B: A chemical substance tested in a laboratory beaker
options.C: The final written report published in a journal
options.D: The budget allocated for purchasing hospital supplies

explanation: Researchers study a sample because it is usually impossible to measure every single person in a target population. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is the purpose of establishing clear inclusion and exclusion criteria?

options.A: To make sure only wealthy patients get selected for trials
options.B: To reduce the total number of hospital beds available
options.C: To prevent doctors from reading the research proposal
options.D: To define precisely who can and cannot safely participate in the study

explanation: Criteria protect patient safety and ensure the studied group matches the exact research question. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h4)

question: What must be obtained from participants before data collection begins?

options.A: Proof of employment
options.B: A financial deposit
options.C: Physician resignation
options.D: Informed consent

explanation: Participants must voluntarily agree to take part after fully understanding what the study involves. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is consistency in data collection so important during the empirical phase?

options.A: It guarantees that every participant will receive financial payment
options.B: It allows researchers to finish their shifts earlier in the day
options.C: It stops patients from asking questions about their treatment
options.D: It prevents errors and ensures measurements are reliable across all participants

explanation: If data is gathered differently for each person, the final results will be skewed and untrustworthy. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h5)

question: What happens during qualitative data analysis?

options.A: Patients fill out numerical rating scales for pain
options.B: Computers calculate complex algebraic formulas and p-values
options.C: Researchers code text to identify recurring themes and patterns
options.D: Blood samples are centrifuged in a hospital laboratory

explanation: Qualitative analysis organizes narrative words and interviews into meaningful categories or themes. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why is it important for researchers to discuss study limitations during data interpretation?

options.A: To prove that their research is completely flawless and superior
options.B: To justify increasing the budget for future research projects
options.C: To confuse readers so they do not question the findings
options.D: To honestly acknowledge any weaknesses or factors that could affect the results

explanation: No study is perfect, and transparency about limitations builds scientific credibility. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary way researchers share their completed findings with the professional community?

options.A: Shredding documents to protect hospital secrets
options.B: Publishing articles in peer-reviewed journals
options.C: Telling patients secretly during hospital discharge
options.D: Posting personal opinions on social media apps

explanation: Peer-reviewed journals are the gold standard for distributing verified research to other professionals. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T1#GNS217_U3_T1_h7)

question: A hospital ward manager reads a newly published study proving a new dressing reduces infection rates. What action represents utilizing this research?

options.A: Scolding staff nurses for not discovering the dressing themselves
