options.C: Takes less than five minutes to finish
options.D: Gives the exact same results every time

explanation: Validity is all about accuracy, meaning the tool actually captures the specific concept being studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h2)

question: A nurse uses a pain scale that somehow measures patient hunger instead of pain. Which quality is this tool lacking?

options.A: Reliability
options.B: Length
options.C: Practicality
options.D: Validity

explanation: When an instrument measures the wrong concept, it lacks validity because it is not capturing what it claims to measure. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h2)

question: Which instrument is best for capturing deep, personal stories from patients about chronic illness?

options.A: Interview guide
options.B: Simple questionnaire
options.C: Blood pressure cuff
options.D: Checklist of bedside actions

explanation: Interview guides allow researchers to ask open-ended questions and explore personal experiences in detail. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h3)

question: A researcher wants to record the exact physical behaviors of nurses during a sterile dressing change. Which instrument should they use?

options.A: Observational checklist
options.B: Structured interview guide
options.C: Patient satisfaction survey
options.D: Biographical questionnaire

explanation: Observational checklists are ideal for watching and recording specific actions as they happen in real time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h3)

question: What is a double-barreled question in a research instrument?

options.A: A question that has more than ten possible answers
options.B: A question written in two different languages
options.C: A question that is asked twice during an interview
options.D: A question that asks about two different things at once

explanation: Double-barreled questions confuse respondents because they combine multiple ideas into a single query. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why is it important to test draft survey questions on a small group before the main study?

options.A: To force participants to agree with the researcher
options.B: To finish the research project much faster
options.C: To catch hidden mistakes and confusing wording
options.D: To make the final paper look longer and better

explanation: Pilot testing helps identify confusing questions and errors before you spend time and resources on the full study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose an observational checklist instead of a patient questionnaire?

options.A: Patients prefer being watched over writing answers
options.B: What people say they do can differ from their actual actions
options.C: Observational checklists are much cheaper to print
options.D: Questionnaires cannot be used in a hospital setting

explanation: Direct observation captures real behavior, avoiding the bias or forgetfulness that comes with self-reporting. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h5)

question: What is a major benefit of using physiological measures like a blood pressure machine in research?

options.A: They eliminate the need for any human researchers
options.B: They cost nothing to purchase and maintain
options.C: They take the place of nursing clinical judgment
options.D: They provide objective data that cannot be falsified by memory

explanation: Physiological tools measure physical states directly, providing reliable, objective data without relying on patient memory. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h5)

question: Which type of validity involves checking if a new tool compares well with an established gold standard?

options.A: Surface validity
options.B: Criterion validity
options.C: Face validity
options.D: Content validity

explanation: Criterion validity is established when a new instrument scores similarly to a trusted, proven gold-standard tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h6)

question: A panel of senior nurses reviews a new questionnaire to see if it covers every aspect of post-operative care. What are they testing?

options.A: Content validity
options.B: Physical durability
options.C: Data entry speed
options.D: Test-retest reliability

explanation: Content validity ensures that the tool covers all important dimensions of the subject being studied. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h6)

question: What statistical value is commonly used to measure the internal consistency of a questionnaire?

options.A: Cronbach's alpha
options.B: Celsius scale
options.C: Body mass index
options.D: P-value index

explanation: Cronbach's alpha is the standard statistical test used to check if items within a scale relate well to one another. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h7)

question: Two clinical supervisors watch the same nursing student perform a procedure and grade them using the same checklist. What are they checking?

options.A: Test-retest validity
options.B: Content consistency
options.C: Inter-rater reliability
options.D: Patient satisfaction

explanation: Inter-rater reliability checks whether different observers get similar scores when using the exact same tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why must researchers follow a standardized procedure during data collection?

options.A: To make the research process take longer
options.B: To avoid getting permission from the hospital
options.C: To ensure patients pay for their participation
options.D: To prevent outside disturbances from ruining results

explanation: Standardized procedures ensure every participant has the same experience, keeping data collection consistent and reliable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the primary reason for keeping completed research questionnaires in a locked cabinet?

options.A: To ensure the forms do not get misplaced by staff
options.B: To make sure nobody steals the paper pens
options.C: To protect patient confidentiality and privacy
options.D: To comply with hospital interior design rules

explanation: Securing completed research documents is an ethical duty to protect participants' private health information. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a questionnaire in nursing research?

options.A: To perform direct physical examinations on patients
options.B: To prescribe medication adjustments based on lab work
options.C: To replace the need for informed consent in a study
options.D: To gather structured data directly from participants

explanation: A questionnaire is specifically designed as a written tool to collect standardized information straight from respondents. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h1)

question: Why do researchers use the exact same questions and words for everyone taking a survey?

options.A: It prevents participants from feeling confused by long medical terms
options.B: It guarantees that every participant will finish the survey faster
options.C: It allows the nurse researcher to change the topic mid-interview
options.D: It ensures all answers can be fairly compared across the group

explanation: Using identical wording means any differences in the responses are due to actual differences between people, not because a question was asked differently. Keep pushing forward! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h1)

question: What kind of survey question gives people a fixed list of choices to pick from?

options.A: Unstructured item
options.B: Open-ended item
options.C: Closed-ended item
options.D: Narrative item

explanation: Closed-ended items restrict answers to predefined options, which makes counting and analyzing the responses much easier for your research project. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h2)

question: A nurse wants to measure patient satisfaction using options from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. Which format should she use?

options.A: Likert scale
options.B: Open-ended essay
options.C: Dichotomous checklist
options.D: Biographical interview

explanation: A Likert scale is designed specifically to measure attitudes and agreement levels across a multi-point scale. Great job learning the research tools! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is a 'double-barreled' question in a research survey?

options.A: A question placed at the very end of a long research tool
options.B: A single question that mistakenly asks about two different things
options.C: A question that offers more than five possible answer choices
options.D: A survey item written in two different languages at once

explanation: Double-barreled questions confuse respondents because they cannot give separate answers to two different ideas packed into one sentence. You'll master questionnaire design in no time! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why is it best to put easy, general questions at the very beginning of a survey?

options.A: To trick the participant into answering difficult items quickly
options.B: To ensure the statistical software can read the demographic data
options.C: To shorten the total amount of time needed for data collection
options.D: To help the participant feel comfortable and build trust

explanation: Starting with gentle, straightforward questions eases anxiety and encourages people to complete the rest of the questionnaire. Brilliant thinking! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h3)

question: In research, what does the 'validity' of a questionnaire mean?

options.A: Whether the tool can be completed in under ten minutes
options.B: Whether the tool measures what it is intended to measure
options.C: Whether the tool was printed on approved institutional paper
options.D: Whether the tool gives the exact same scores on repeat testing

explanation: Validity checks if your questions are truly capturing the specific concept or variable you set out to study. You're building solid clinical research skills! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h4)

question: What does it mean if a research questionnaire is described as 'reliable'?

options.A: It successfully measures complex human emotions accurately
options.B: It has been approved by the hospital ethics committee
options.C: It gives consistent results when used repeatedly over time
options.D: It is completely free from any potential ethical violations

explanation: Reliability is all about consistency. A reliable tool yields similar scores when conditions remain stable. Keep up the great work! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h4)

question: What is a major downside of using online questionnaires for hospital patients?

options.A: They prevent researchers from collecting any numerical data
options.B: They force patients to answer every question before submitting
options.C: They always cost significantly more than printed paper surveys
options.D: They may exclude patients who lack internet access or devices

explanation: The digital divide means older or lower-income patients might not have the technology required to complete online forms. Excellent real-world nursing perspective! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which way of giving out a survey lets a nurse directly clarify confusing items for the respondent?

options.A: Anonymous drop-off boxes
options.B: Face-to-face administration
options.C: Unmonitored online web links
options.D: Standard postal mail surveys

explanation: When you are present during survey administration, you can immediately explain what a question means if the participant looks confused. Spot on! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h5)

question: What is the main reason for running a 'pilot test' on a questionnaire before a big study?

options.A: To identify and fix problems before the main study begins
options.B: To permanently replace the need for an ethics review
options.C: To publish the final research results ahead of schedule
options.D: To recruit participants who will drop out of the study

explanation: Pilot testing lets researchers spot unclear wording or formatting errors on a small group before spending resources on the full study. Smart thinking! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h6)

question: Who should ideally test out a draft questionnaire in the pre-testing phase?

options.A: Only senior professors who have published many research papers
options.B: Patients who have already completed the final main survey
options.C: Hospital accountants who manage the research funding budget
options.D: People who share similar characteristics with your target study group

explanation: Pre-testing works best when done with individuals who resemble your actual study participants so they can give realistic feedback. You're doing brilliantly! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h6)

question: What must a participant give before answering a research questionnaire?

options.A: Proof of health insurance
options.B: A physician's referral letter
options.C: A notarized identity card
options.D: Informed consent

explanation: Participants must voluntarily agree to take part after being fully informed about the study's purpose. Ethical nursing practice starts here! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is the main difference between anonymity and confidentiality in research?

options.A: Anonymity is only required for online surveys, while confidentiality is for paper surveys
options.B: Anonymity means no identifying data is collected, while confidentiality protects data that is collected
options.C: Anonymity allows researchers to share names, while confidentiality stops all sharing
options.D: There is no real difference between the two terms in nursing research

explanation: An anonymous survey collects zero names or identifiers, whereas a confidential survey collects names or codes but promises to keep them strictly private. Well understood! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is a major advantage of using questionnaires in nursing research?

options.A: They guarantee a 100 percent response rate from participants
options.B: They can efficiently gather data from large numbers of people
options.C: They completely eliminate the possibility of human bias
options.D: They allow researchers to perform deep physical exams

explanation: Questionnaires can be distributed widely via mail or the internet, making it easy to collect data from large populations quickly. Excellent job! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical limitation of questionnaire-based studies?

options.A: The potential for respondents to misunderstand written items
options.B: The lack of opportunity to ask follow-up probing questions
options.C: The ability to immediately observe complex clinical healing processes
options.D: The risk of receiving very low response rates from participants

explanation: Questionnaires collect self-reported written data; they do not allow a nurse to physically observe clinical healing processes firsthand. You are crushing these questions! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T22#GNS224_U1_T22_h8)

question: What is a research checklist mainly used for in nursing studies?

options.A: To schedule nursing staff shifts on the ward
options.B: To systematically record observations and data
options.C: To prescribe medication dosages to patients
options.D: To diagnose complex medical conditions

explanation: Think of a checklist as your organized guide! It gives you a structured way to observe and tick off items uniformly during a study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers love using checklists instead of messy, freehand notes?

options.A: Checklists reduce missed details and ensure consistency
options.B: Checklists completely eliminate the need for human observers
options.C: Checklists are the only tool allowed by ethical boards
options.D: Checklists take no time at all to design or implement

explanation: Busy hospital shifts can be chaotic. A good checklist keeps your data uniform and stops you from forgetting important details! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h1)

question: How do checklists help prevent unfair or biased observations in a study?

options.A: By allowing the researcher to change the questions daily
options.B: By evaluating every participant using the same criteria
options.C: By removing human judgment completely from the process
options.D: By hiding the study goals from the clinical staff

explanation: When everyone is measured against the exact same standard, personal opinions won't sway your results. Fair and square! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h2)

question: What happens when a research checklist turns your observations into simple checkmarks?

options.A: It turns descriptive notes into countable data for statistics
options.B: It automatically publishes the findings in a journal
options.C: It removes all potential errors from the research process
options.D: It changes qualitative research into a medical prescription

explanation: Tick marks make counting things super easy, which lets you run simple math and stats on your findings later. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h2)

question: Which checklist type is best for checking if specific steps are done in the right order?

options.A: Task or process checklist
options.B: Unstructured narrative log
options.C: Biographical data form
options.D: Patient satisfaction survey

explanation: A process checklist breaks down a procedure step-by-step so you can tick them off as they happen in real-time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h3)

question: You want to score how well nursing students perform sterile wound dressings in simulation. Which tool fits best?

options.A: An open-ended diary for students to write about their feelings
options.B: A simple task checklist that only records yes or no without scoring
options.C: A demographic questionnaire about the students' previous degrees
options.D: An evaluation or rating checklist to score the quality of performance

explanation: A rating checklist lets you assess how *well* a skill was done, going beyond a simple yes-or-no tick. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h3)

question: What is the final practical step you should take before using a brand new checklist in a major study?

options.A: Translate the checklist into three new languages
options.B: Publish the checklist in a nursing journal
options.C: Pilot test the draft in a small trial run
options.D: File the checklist away in a locked cabinet

explanation: Always test-run your tool first! A pilot test helps catch confusing questions or missing steps before you start the real study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h4)

question: Why is defining your research goal the most crucial first step when designing a checklist?

options.A: It guarantees that patients will agree to participate in the study
options.B: It eliminates the need for any literature review during the project
options.C: It determines the final statistical software the study will use
options.D: It guides which specific variables and items need to be included

explanation: When you know your exact goal, every single item you put on that checklist will directly serve your research purpose. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h4)

question: What does 'validity' mean when we talk about a research checklist?

options.A: Two different nurses get the exact same score every time
options.B: Patients find the checklist easy to read and understand
options.C: The checklist is printed on high-quality paper for clinical use
options.D: The checklist measures what it is actually supposed to measure

explanation: Validity is all about accuracy. Does the tool actually capture the exact thing you set out to study? [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h5)

question: How do researchers usually test the inter-rater reliability of an observational checklist?

options.A: By having two observers use the same checklist and comparing their scores
options.B: By checking if the literature review matches the study hypothesis
options.C: By asking patients if they enjoyed filling out the research forms
options.D: By measuring how long it takes to complete the checklist items

explanation: Inter-rater reliability checks if two different people using the same tool will get matching results. Teamwork and consistency! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h5)

question: What is a common danger when researchers use very long or complex checklists during busy ward shifts?

options.A: Observer fatigue leading to rushed or guessed answers
options.B: Automatic rejection of the study by the ethics committee
options.C: Immediate breakdown of hospital computer networks
options.D: Patients refusing to take their prescribed medications

explanation: Keep it concise! When tools are too long and staff are tired, they lose focus and might just start guessing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h6)

question: Why is pre-training essential for nurses who will use research checklists on the ward?

options.A: To teach them how to perform advanced surgical operations
options.B: To make sure they spend less than one minute on each patient
options.C: To prevent the hospital from hiring outside research assistants
options.D: To ensure everyone interprets and records items in the same way

explanation: Training gets everyone on the same page, ensuring your data stays reliable no matter who fills out the form. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h6)

question: Which of the following is a major drawback or limitation of using research checklists?

options.A: They cost more money than any other research tool
options.B: They are completely impossible to analyze statistically
options.C: They take months of training to read and write
options.D: They can oversimplify complex clinical situations

explanation: Checklists are great, but ticking boxes can sometimes strip away the rich details of a complex clinical scenario. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT an advantage of using a checklist in nursing research?

options.A: Producing structured data that is easy to score
options.B: Being quick and straightforward to administer
options.C: Providing deep, emotional life stories of patients
options.D: Reducing subjective wandering during clinical observation

explanation: Checklists capture neat, measurable data—they aren't designed to tell deep, open-ended emotional stories. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T23#GNS224_U1_T23_h7)

question: As a nurse researcher, why would you choose to use qualitative interviews?

options.A: To measure exact physiological vital signs over time
options.B: To explore deep human experiences and personal perspectives
options.C: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on large populations
options.D: To calculate statistical averages of hospital stays

explanation: You've got this! Qualitative interviews are all about listening to patients' stories and feelings, rather than just crunching numbers. It's the human side of nursing research! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h1)

question: When studying how patients cope with long-term illness, why are interviews often better than rigid surveys?

options.A: Interviews allow participants to explain things in their own words
options.B: Surveys are too expensive to print out in hospital wards
options.C: Interviews do not require any ethical review board approval
options.D: Surveys only work when patients are unconscious

explanation: Spot on! People aren't checkboxes. Letting patients talk freely gives you rich insights that a standard survey would completely miss. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h1)

question: Which interview style uses a flexible guide while letting you ask spontaneous follow-up questions?

options.A: Semi-structured interview
options.B: Unstructured interview
options.C: Blinded clinical interview
options.D: Structured interview

explanation: Great thinking! 'Semi-structured' means you have a helpful roadmap of topics, but you're free to follow interesting details as the patient shares them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h2)

question: You want to ask ten exact admission questions across five different hospitals without changing a single word. Which format fits best?

options.A: Open-ended dialogue
options.B: Structured interview
options.C: Unstructured interview
options.D: Semi-structured interview

explanation: You nailed it! A structured interview is rigid on purpose—it keeps every single question identical so your data stays consistent across different sites. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h2)

question: When drafting questions for an interview guide, which type of question should you definitely avoid?

options.A: Open-ended questions
options.B: Broad introductory questions
options.C: Clear and simple questions
options.D: Leading questions

explanation: Well done! Leading questions secretly push the patient toward a specific answer (like 'You take your drugs on time, right?'). We want honest, unbiased stories! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h3)

question: Why is it best to kick off a research interview with a gentle, friendly icebreaker?

options.A: To test if the audio recorder is working properly
options.B: To help build trust and put the participant at ease
options.C: To quickly finish the interview before shift change
options.D: To trick the participant into sharing secrets

explanation: Exactly! Hospital studies can feel intimidating to patients. A warm, easy start helps them relax and feel safe with you. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h3)

question: Before you walk up to patients in a ward to chat with them for a study, what must you secure first?

options.A: Permission from the patient's family members only
options.B: A personal loan from the hospital bank
options.C: Formal institutional and ethical approval
options.D: Complete control over hospital bed assignments

explanation: You got it! Protecting patients is our number one priority. Ethical clearance is non-negotiable before any research begins. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h4)

question: You need to interview a recovering surgical patient on the ward. Where is the best spot to sit down with them?

options.A: At the main hospital cafeteria during lunch hour
options.B: In a busy hallway right outside the nurses' station
options.C: In a private, quiet room away from routine ward noise
options.D: Inside a crowded emergency department waiting area

explanation: Perfect! Privacy and quiet protect the patient's confidentiality and help them speak openly without feeling exposed. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h4)

question: Why is using strategic silence during an interview actually a great communication tool?

options.A: It shows the researcher is bored with the conversation
options.B: It gives the participant time to think and share deeper thoughts
options.C: It signals that the interview is officially over
options.D: It forces the participant to change the topic immediately

explanation: Spot on! Silence can feel awkward, but giving patients a moment to breathe lets them process deep emotions and share truly meaningful insights. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h5)

question: How does taking time to build good rapport with a patient help your qualitative interview?

options.A: It creates trust so the participant feels safe sharing honest feelings
options.B: It shortens the time needed to record and transcribe audio
options.C: It makes the participant tell the researcher what they want to hear
options.D: It prevents the need for any ethical consent forms

explanation: Brilliant! When patients know you genuinely care and won't judge them, they open up with their true experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h5)

question: Which of these statements about informed consent in qualitative interviews is FALSE?

options.A: It ensures participants know what the study is about
options.B: It protects the voluntary nature of participation
options.C: It only matters before the interview starts and is then forgotten
options.D: It is a continuous process that can be withdrawn at any time

explanation: You got it! Consent isn't just a paper signed at the beginning—a patient can change their mind and step out of the study at any point. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h6)

question: A patient starts crying while talking about a painful hospital memory during an interview. What should you do first?

options.A: Pause the interview, offer compassionate support, and check if they want to stop
options.B: Turn off the audio recorder and scold the patient for getting upset
options.C: Immediately ignore the tears and rush to finish the next question
options.D: Report the patient to the medical team for psychiatric evaluation

explanation: Compassion over everything! Always put the patient's emotional well-being ahead of your research notes. You're a nurse first. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h6)

question: What does a 'verbatim transcription' of a recorded interview mean?

options.A: Translating the interview into a foreign language
options.B: Converting audio files into exact written text word-for-word
options.C: Summarizing the main points into a single paragraph
options.D: Deleting all pauses and laughs from the recording

explanation: Spot on! Verbatim means capturing every single spoken word precisely as it was said to keep your research accurate. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h7)

question: Why must you store your interview audio files and transcripts in password-protected digital folders?

options.A: To prevent accidental loss of data and protect patient confidentiality
options.B: To speed up the internet connection in the research office
options.C: To make the files look more professional for publishing
options.D: To allow the general public to read private hospital stories

explanation: Exactly right! Patient stories are deeply personal, and keeping digital files secure is a core part of ethical nursing practice. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h7)

question: What is 'member checking' when doing qualitative research?

options.A: Sharing findings back with participants to confirm accuracy
options.B: Testing the audio recorder battery before an interview
options.C: Reviewing staff membership lists for the research team
options.D: Checking if participants paid their hospital bills

explanation: Brilliant! Member checking means going back to your participants to say, 'Did I get your story right?' It ensures your interpretation is honest and true. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h8)

question: Why do qualitative researchers keep a reflexive journal throughout their study?

options.A: To monitor and reflect on their own personal biases
options.B: To write personal diary entries about their coworkers
options.C: To record daily weather patterns in the hospital ward
options.D: To keep track of how much money they spent on printing

explanation: You nailed it! Reflexivity helps us check our own personal opinions and background so we don't accidentally twist what our patients are telling us. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T24#GNS224_U1_T24_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of observation as a data collection method?

options.A: Recording behaviors and events as they naturally occur
options.B: Asking participants to fill out a detailed questionnaire
options.C: Conducting formal interviews with patient family members
options.D: Reviewing past medical records in the hospital archive

explanation: Observation involves watching and recording real-time actions and conditions without necessarily asking questions or altering the environment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h1)

question: Why is observation often more reliable than interviews in research?

options.A: It allows researchers to control what the participants say
options.B: It takes much less time and fewer resources to complete
options.C: It captures actual behavior rather than just reported behavior
options.D: It is completely free of any human bias or error

explanation: People sometimes misremember or forget details in interviews, but direct observation lets you see what is truly happening in real time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h1)

question: What type of observation happens when a researcher joins a group to experience their daily routine firsthand?

options.A: Non-participant observation
options.B: Participant observation
options.C: Structured observation
options.D: Laboratory observation

explanation: You got it! In 'participant observation', the researcher actively joins the community to get an inside perspective. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h2)

question: A nurse sits quietly in the corner of a pediatric playroom to watch children interact without joining in or altering the setting. What kind of observation is this?

options.A: Structured experimental trial
options.B: Non-participant observation
options.C: Unstructured clinical interview
options.D: Participant observation

explanation: Remaining detached and watching without direct interaction defines non-participant observation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h2)

question: Which observational tool is best used to grade the quality or frequency of a specific behavior?

options.A: Simple checklist
options.B: Consent form
options.C: Rating scale
options.D: Archival record

explanation: Think of a rating scale as a grading tool. It lets you measure the degree or quality of an action, rather than just noting if it happened or not. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h3)

question: A nursing researcher wants to mark down the exact presence or absence of hand hygiene steps among ward staff during a shift. Which tool should they use?

options.A: Audio recording
options.B: Checklist
options.C: Unstructured narrative
options.D: Rating scale

explanation: Checklists are ideal for recording whether specific, distinct actions occurred or did not occur. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h3)

question: In research, what do we call the 'Hawthorne effect'?

options.A: Patients refusing to give consent for data collection in the ward
options.B: Data getting lost because field notes were not written down promptly
options.C: The researcher missing key events due to fatigue during a long shift
options.D: People changing their behavior because they know they are being watched

explanation: Spot on! The Hawthorne effect happens naturally because humans tend to act differently when they realize someone is watching them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h4)

question: What is a major advantage of using observation instead of questionnaires?

options.A: It guarantees that participants will never experience anxiety
options.B: It is completely immune to any form of human judgment error
options.C: It records actual behavior rather than self-reported claims
options.D: It requires zero preparation or specialized recording tools

explanation: Exactly! People might say one thing in a questionnaire, but observation lets you see what they actually do in practice. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h4)

question: What term describes two different observers getting similar results when watching the same event?

options.A: The Hawthorne effect
options.B: Participant bias
options.C: Inter-rater reliability
options.D: Structured validity

explanation: Well done! 'Inter-rater reliability' simply means different observers agree and are consistent in how they score what they see. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h5)

question: Why is ethical clearance and consent so important even in observational nursing studies?

options.A: To protect patient privacy and respect autonomy
options.B: To eliminate all possibilities of observer bias completely
options.C: To ensure the hospital receives more funding for research
options.D: To prevent the researcher from getting tired during shifts

explanation: Spot on! Even when we are just watching, we must always respect patients' privacy rights and personal autonomy. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T25#GNS224_U1_T25_h5)

question: In nursing research, what does 'validity' simply mean?

options.A: How truly a study measures what it claims to measure
options.B: How fast a computer can run the data
options.C: Whether the paper was published in a big journal
options.D: How many patients took part in the study

explanation: Think of validity as truthfulness! It just checks if the research tool or study is actually measuring what it says it is measuring. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h1)

question: Why is it super important to check if a research study is valid before using its findings on your hospital ward?

options.A: To make sure nurses get extra credit for reading
options.B: To make sure the hospital buys the newest equipment
options.C: To prevent using flawed ideas that could harm patients
options.D: To save money on printing out research papers

explanation: As future nurses, our top priority is patient safety. If research is flawed, applying it on the ward could lead to poor patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h1)

question: What is the main focus of 'internal validity' in a research study?

options.A: Proving that the treatment actually caused the change in the patient
options.B: Checking if the lab thermometer was working well
options.C: Counting how many student nurses helped collect data
options.D: Seeing if the results apply to patients in other countries

explanation: Internal validity is all about cause and effect inside the study. Did our nursing intervention really cause that improvement, or was it something else? [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h2)

question: A patient drops out halfway through a six-month nursing study on chronic pain. What is this called in research terms?

options.A: Testing
options.B: Attrition
options.C: Maturation
options.D: History

explanation: Attrition happens when participants leave or drop out before a study ends. It can mess up our data, so researchers always watch out for it! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h2)

question: What does 'external validity' deal with?

options.A: How fast data goes into the hospital computer
options.B: How well patients understand their consent forms
options.C: Whether the study results can apply to other patients in the real world
options.D: How accurate the thermometers are in the laboratory

explanation: External validity asks: 'If this worked in a tiny research lab, will it also work for our patients out here on the busy hospital wards?' [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h3)

question: A researcher tests a new diet only on young male athletes in Lagos. Why might this study have low external validity for older women in a rural clinic?

options.A: The laboratory scales were probably out of date
options.B: The researchers forgot to check blood pressures
options.C: The study group does not represent the broader patient population
options.D: The study lacked a budget for food

explanation: You can't easily apply results from young athletes to everyone else! External validity depends on whether your study group actually looks like the wider community. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h3)

question: What is 'construct validity' trying to measure?

options.A: The total amount of grant money given for the project
options.B: The physical weight of hospital equipment
options.C: The exact number of people who filled out a form
options.D: Invisible human experiences like pain, anxiety, or depression

explanation: Construct validity checks if our survey or test successfully captures big, invisible concepts like how anxious or in pain a patient really is. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h4)

question: A nurse designs a questionnaire for depression, but the questions only ask about lack of sleep. What is the main problem here?

options.A: The statistical power is too strong
options.B: Too many patients dropped out
options.C: The external validity is too high
options.D: Poor construct validity because depression is more than just bad sleep

explanation: Depression is a broad condition. If a test only looks at sleep, it misses the big picture—showing poor construct validity! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h4)

question: What is the main concern of 'statistical conclusion validity'?

options.A: Whether the hospital management approved the budget
options.B: Whether the results can be used in other countries
options.C: Whether participants signed their consent forms
options.D: Whether the right math and statistical tests were used to find a true link

explanation: This type of validity makes sure the researchers didn't use the wrong math formulas, so we can trust that their numbers actually mean something. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h5)

question: Why can having a very small number of patients (sample size) ruin statistical conclusion validity?

options.A: It makes it hard for the math to catch real differences between groups
options.B: It makes the external validity way too broad
options.C: It automatically makes patients run away
options.D: It proves the whole theory is wrong

explanation: When your sample size is too tiny, statistical tests struggle to spot real changes, meaning you might miss an important finding. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h5)

question: Why do researchers use random assignment when setting up a clinical study?

options.A: To lower the cost of buying hospital drugs
options.B: To guarantee the study applies to the whole world
options.C: To finish the study as quickly as possible
options.D: To balance out differences between patients and protect internal validity

explanation: Randomly putting patients into groups helps ensure both groups start off similar, so we know the treatment—not patient differences—made the change. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h6)

question: In a drug trial, why do researchers use 'blinding' (hiding who gets the real drug or a fake sugar pill)?

options.A: To make the computer software run faster
options.B: To prove the theoretical construct is correct
options.C: To make sure everyone drops out at the same time
options.D: To stop people's expectations from messing up the results

explanation: If patients or nurses know who got the real medicine, they might act differently or judge results with bias. Blinding keeps everything fair and honest! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h6)

question: What must a nurse do before changing how they care for patients based on a new research paper?

options.A: Carefully check the study's validity and methods first
options.B: Wait ten whole years before taking any action
options.C: Just assume it's true because it was printed in a magazine
options.D: Ask every single hospital patient for their permission

explanation: Evidence-based practice means we don't just follow every new trend blindly; we appraise the research to make sure it's solid and safe. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a helpful question to ask when checking if a research study is good enough for your ward?

options.A: Can these findings actually work on our specific patient ward?
options.B: How many awards has the lead author won for writing?
options.C: Did the researchers use a good tool to measure the problem?
options.D: Was the number of patients large enough for good results?

explanation: Personal awards don't make science valid! We care about proper sample sizes, good measurement tools, and real clinical usefulness. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T26#GNS224_U1_T26_h7)

question: In research, what do we mean when we say a tool is 'reliable'?

options.A: How easy the questionnaire is for elderly patients to read
options.B: How fast the researcher can collect data from patients
options.C: How consistently the tool produces the same results
options.D: Whether the tool measures what it is supposed to measure

explanation: Think of reliability like a dependable weighing scale—if you step on it five times in a row and get the exact same weight, it's reliable (even if it needs calibration later!). It's all about consistency. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h1)

question: Why is high reliability so important for our nursing research tools?

options.A: It proves the researchers spent enough money on equipment
options.B: It ensures study results are free from random measurement errors
options.C: It guarantees that patients will recover faster on the ward
options.D: It stops patients from dropping out of clinical trials early

explanation: Reliable tools cut out the guesswork and random noise. When we use them, we can trust our data reflects what's truly happening on the ward! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h1)

question: What is the main focus of 'validity' when creating a research tool?

options.A: Whether the tool gives the exact same score every single time
options.B: How many patients can complete the form in ten minutes
options.C: How cheap the research instrument is to buy in bulk
options.D: Whether the tool measures what it is supposed to measure

explanation: Validity is about hitting the bullseye! If you want to measure patient anxiety, a valid tool actually captures anxiety, not physical pain or hunger. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h2)

question: Imagine a BP machine reads 200/120 mmHg three times in a row for a healthy person whose real BP is 120/80 mmHg. How would you describe this tool?

options.A: Both high reliability and high validity
options.B: High reliability but low validity
options.C: Both low reliability and low validity
options.D: Low reliability and high validity

explanation: It gave the exact same wrong number repeatedly, so it's consistent (reliable), but completely off the mark (invalid). Classic case of high reliability, low validity! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h2)

question: What does 'test-retest reliability' check in a study?

options.A: Stability of scores over time
options.B: Agreement between two different observers
options.C: Equivalence of two different questionnaire versions
options.D: Internal similarity of survey questions

explanation: Spot on! Test-retest simply means giving the same test to the same people at two different times to see if the scores stay stable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h3)

question: If a nurse researcher tests patients with a pain scale twice, why is a very short time interval between tests sometimes a bad idea?

options.A: The patients will experience severe physical exhaustion
options.B: Hospital management will not approve the extra paperwork
options.C: Patients might remember and repeat their previous answers
options.D: The thermometer or scale will lose its electrical charge

explanation: This is called recall bias! If patients just remember what they wrote five minutes ago, they'll copy it, making the tool look more reliable than it actually is. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h3)

question: Which statistical test do researchers commonly use to check internal consistency?

options.A: Chi-square test
options.B: Student's t-test
options.C: Pearson correlation
options.D: Cronbach's alpha

explanation: Cronbach's alpha is the go-to statistical number for checking if all the questions in your survey hang together nicely to measure the same thing. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h4)

question: A researcher gets a Cronbach's alpha of 0.82 for a new nursing burnout scale. What does this tell us?

options.A: The responses given by the patients are completely invalid
options.B: The questionnaire is unstable and changes too much over time
options.C: The questions on the scale measure completely different traits
options.D: The scale has strong internal consistency

explanation: Any alpha score above 0.70 is usually a green light showing your questions work well together as a team! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h4)

question: What is the simple difference between inter-rater and intra-rater reliability?

options.A: Inter-rater uses computers, while intra-rater relies entirely on patient self-reporting
options.B: Inter-rater measures time, while intra-rater measures physical instrument weight
options.C: Inter-rater looks at agreement between different observers, while intra-rater looks at consistency within a single observer
options.D: There is no real difference, as both terms mean the exact same thing in research

explanation: Remember the prefixes: 'Inter-' means between different people (two nurses comparing notes), while 'intra-' means within the same person grading things over time. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h5)

question: Two clinical nurses independently score a patient's wound healing using the same chart. What type of reliability are they testing?

options.A: Parallel forms reliability
options.B: Test-retest reliability
options.C: Inter-rater reliability
options.D: Internal consistency reliability

explanation: Since two separate raters are checking their agreement on the same patient, it's inter-rater reliability in action! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h5)

question: What is the main goal of using 'parallel forms reliability'?

options.A: To determine if survey questions relate to the same overall topic
options.B: To check if a single nurse can grade wounds consistently over days
options.C: To see if two different versions of a test yield equivalent results
options.D: To measure how much patients remember from their first clinic visit

explanation: Parallel forms just means Version A and Version B of a test match up equally well in measuring the same concept. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h6)

question: Why would an educator use parallel forms reliability for a student exam?

options.A: To eliminate the need for statistical software like SPSS during analysis
options.B: To ensure patients do not experience physical fatigue during long interviews
options.C: To prevent students from copying answers by using two equivalent test versions
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of printing paper questionnaires in the hospital

explanation: Having two fair, equivalent versions of a test lets you switch up questions between rows in a crowded hall without sacrificing test quality! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h6)

question: A research group finds a questionnaire that was super reliable in the US ten years ago. Why must they test its reliability again for a new local study?

options.A: Hospital ethics committees require a new test to pay the researchers
options.B: Published research papers automatically expire after five years
options.C: Cultural differences and demographics can change how the tool performs
options.D: Statistical formulas change every decade to match new computer systems

explanation: Reliability isn't a permanent stamp of approval. A tool that works great in one culture or setting might need re-testing to prove it fits a different local population. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h7)

question: In a formal research report, which section will you find the reliability scores of the measurement tools?

options.A: Acknowledgements
options.B: References
options.C: Methods
options.D: Introduction

explanation: The Methods section is the researcher's 'recipe book'—it's where they explain every tool used and how reliable it was. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T27#GNS224_U1_T27_h7)

question: Think of a research design as a step-by-step plan. What is its main job in nursing?

options.A: To secure ethical approval from the hospital board
options.B: To calculate the exact financial cost of a hospital study
options.C: To write the final reference list for a journal article
options.D: To act as a blueprint for answering a clinical question

explanation: Spot on! Just like building a house needs a good plan, a research design is your overall framework that guides how you answer a specific clinical question. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why is picking the right research design so important for your everyday patient care?

options.A: It guarantees that every patient will recover quickly
options.B: It stops nurses from having to read previous literature
options.C: It ensures findings are valid and useful for patient care
options.D: It eliminates the need for any statistical data analysis

explanation: You got it! A solid design cuts down errors so the evidence we find is safe and reliable enough to use right at the bedside. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h1)

question: When you hear 'quantitative research', what kind of data immediately comes to mind?

options.A: Unstructured audio recordings of interviews
options.B: Numerical data and measurable variables
options.C: Handwritten patient diary entries
options.D: Detailed personal stories and life histories

explanation: Think 'Q for Quantity'! Quantitative research is all about numbers, measurements, and stats to find answers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h2)

question: When would a nurse researcher decide to use a quantitative design?

options.A: When writing a narrative history of nursing education
options.B: When measuring the exact change in blood glucose levels
options.C: When exploring the deep emotional meaning of grief
options.D: When observing unspoken cultural rituals in a community

explanation: Awesome! Because blood glucose can be counted and measured in numbers, it's a perfect fit for a quantitative study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main goal when using a qualitative research design?

options.A: Human experiences and subjective meanings
options.B: Exact mathematical measurements of organs
options.C: Statistical probability and sample size formulas
options.D: Controlled laboratory drug trials

explanation: Spot on! Qualitative research focuses on words, stories, and feelings to understand how people experience their world. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which of these topics calls for a qualitative design?

options.A: The effect of a specific dose of paracetamol on fever
options.B: The exact recovery time after an appendectomy
options.C: The daily emotional coping strategies of cancer survivors
options.D: The percentage of hospital staff who wash their hands

explanation: Brilliant! Exploring how someone feels and copes means listening to their personal story—classic qualitative territory. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h3)

question: What key feature is always present in a true experiment, but often missing in a quasi-experiment?

options.A: Formulation of a clear research question
options.B: Measurement of dependent variables
options.C: Review by an ethics committee
options.D: Random assignment of subjects to groups

explanation: You nailed it. True experiments randomly toss participants into groups to keep things fair and balanced. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h4)

question: A nurse wants to test a new handwashing routine on two existing hospital wards without disrupting shift schedules. Which design fits best?

options.A: Quasi-experimental design
options.B: Historical research design
options.C: Phenomenological design
options.D: True experimental design

explanation: Spot on! When you have to use existing groups (like pre-formed wards) instead of mixing everyone randomly, you are doing a quasi-experiment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the big giveaway that a study is non-experimental?

options.A: The researcher does not manipulate any variables
options.B: Participants are randomly assigned to a treatment
options.C: A new drug is tested on a control group
options.D: Data is collected exclusively through interviews

explanation: Correct! In non-experimental studies, you just observe what is happening naturally without changing or meddling with anything. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why would a nurse researcher go for a correlational design?

options.A: To randomly assign patients to different hospital diets
options.B: To prove that variable A causes variable B to change
options.C: To test the effectiveness of a brand-new surgical tool
options.D: To explore the relationship between two existing variables

explanation: You got it! Correlation checks how two things relate to each other (like stress and lack of sleep), without claiming one directly causes the other. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h5)

question: As the name suggests, what does a 'mixed methods' research design mix together?

options.A: Experimental and historical approaches
options.B: Inpatient and outpatient clinical data
options.C: Quantitative and qualitative approaches
options.D: Animal studies and laboratory testing

explanation: Easy peasy! It mixes numbers (quantitative) with words and stories (qualitative) to get the best of both worlds. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the greatest superpower of using a mixed methods design in nursing?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any statistical software programs
options.B: It provides a more complete and thorough picture of a clinical problem
options.C: It is always cheaper and faster to execute than other designs
options.D: It completely removes all forms of bias from the study

explanation: Spot on! By combining hard numbers with real human experiences, you get a much richer understanding of a health issue. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h6)

question: When picking a research design, what should be your number one guide?

options.A: The specific nature of the research question
options.B: The availability of colorful presentation software
options.C: The length of the reference list in textbooks
options.D: The personal preference of the hospital director

explanation: Correct! Always let your research question drive the bus—it tells you what kind of answer you need, which points straight to the right design. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why might a nurse researcher choose an observation study instead of an experiment for ethical reasons?

options.A: Observational studies cost more money to run
options.B: It is unethical to deliberately expose patients to harm
options.C: Hospital management bans all experimental laboratory work
options.D: Patients prefer answering surveys over taking medications

explanation: You nailed it! Patient safety comes first. If an experiment puts participants at risk, we cannot ethically test it directly on them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T3#GNS224_U1_T3_h7)

question: In quantitative research, what is the main type of data you collect?

options.A: Numerical data
options.B: Descriptive text
options.C: Personal stories
options.D: Audio recordings

explanation: Think numbers and measurements! Quantitative research is all about gathering figures to spot patterns and trends. You've got this! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why do quantitative researchers try to remain completely neutral and detached from their study participants?

options.A: To avoid having to write detailed nursing care plans
options.B: To prevent personal bias from affecting the study results
options.C: To make it easier to recruit busy hospital staff
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of running the project

explanation: Staying objective ensures the data truly reflects reality, rather than what the researcher hopes or wishes to see. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h1)

question: What are the three core elements that make a study a true experimental design?

options.A: Manipulation, control, and randomization
options.B: Sampling, blinding, and qualitative coding
options.C: Observation, interview, and transcription
options.D: Surveying, coding, and theme generation

explanation: A true experiment needs these three: you manipulate a variable, control outside factors, and randomly assign your participants. Great revision practice! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: A nurse researcher assigns hospital wards to receive a new handwashing training program by drawing lots. What experimental element is this?

options.A: Randomization
options.B: Manipulation
options.C: Data saturation
options.D: Blinding

explanation: Drawing lots means choice is left entirely to chance—that is classic randomization in action! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h2)

question: What key feature is missing in a quasi-experimental design that you would find in a true experiment?

options.A: Random assignment of participants
options.B: An independent variable
options.C: Measurement tools
options.D: Any form of clinical intervention

explanation: Quasi-experiments test interventions and compare groups, but they skip random assignment because it's often not practical in real hospitals. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why do nurse researchers often choose quasi-experimental designs instead of true experiments in actual clinical settings?

options.A: Hospital management refuses to let nurses use numerical data collection tools
options.B: True experiments are entirely illegal in clinical nursing environments
options.C: Quasi-experimental studies require no ethical approval or patient consent
options.D: It is often impossible to randomly assign patients to groups in a real hospital setting

explanation: In real-world wards, we work with existing groups of patients and staff, making strict random assignment tricky or impossible. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is the main feature of a non-experimental research design?

options.A: The researcher does not manipulate any variables
options.B: Data is collected exclusively through open-ended interviews
options.C: The study takes place inside a controlled laboratory
options.D: Participants are randomly assigned to treatment groups

explanation: In non-experimental studies, you simply observe and measure things as they naturally are without stepping in to change them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: A researcher wants to see if night-shift fatigue relates to medication errors among nurses, without changing their shifts. What design is this?

options.A: Historical qualitative
options.B: True experimental
options.C: Non-experimental
options.D: Quasi-experimental

explanation: Spot on! Because work schedules aren't being altered or manipulated, it's a non-experimental study observing everyday realities. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h4)

question: What do we call the outcome variable that a researcher measures to see the effect of an intervention?

options.A: Extraneous variable
options.B: Dependent variable
options.C: Demographic variable
options.D: Independent variable

explanation: The dependent variable 'depends' on the changes you make. It is the final outcome you measure! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: A study tests if a new low-salt diet lowers blood pressure in hypertensive patients. What is the independent variable?

options.A: The patient's blood pressure
options.B: The hospital reading room
options.C: The patient's age and weight
options.D: The low-salt diet

explanation: The independent variable is the intervention or action introduced by the researcher—in this case, the special diet. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h5)

question: In quantitative research, what does 'reliability' mean for a measurement tool?

options.A: Freedom from ethical violations
options.B: Generalizability to outside hospital populations
options.C: Accuracy in measuring the intended concept
options.D: Consistency of measurement scores over time

explanation: Reliability is all about consistency. If you use the tool again under the same conditions, you should get similar, steady results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which statement describes a study with good external validity?

options.A: The measurement tool produced the exact same score on repeated testing
options.B: The researchers strictly controlled all extraneous variables in the lab
options.C: The sample size was large enough to calculate a valid percentage
options.D: The results can be safely generalized to patients in other healthcare settings

explanation: Think of external validity as your study's passport—it means the findings can travel out of the lab and apply to real patients elsewhere. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which board must review and approve any research involving human participants before data collection starts?

options.A: Institutional Review Board
options.B: Hospital Maintenance Committee
options.C: Financial Audit Committee
options.D: Nursing Licensing Board

explanation: The IRB acts as a safety shield, checking research plans to protect human participants from harm. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: When getting informed consent from a patient for a research study, which of these actions is completely unacceptable?

options.A: Threatening to withhold routine nursing care if the patient refuses to join
options.B: Explaining both the potential risks and benefits of the study clearly
options.C: Ensuring the patient knows they can withdraw at any time without penalty
options.D: Allowing adequate time for the patient to ask questions about the project

explanation: Research participation must always be 100% voluntary. You can never use basic patient care as a weapon or a tool for coercion! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T4#GNS224_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of qualitative research in nursing?

options.A: Calculating patient mortality rates
options.B: Understanding human experiences and meanings
options.C: Measuring exact physiological vital signs
options.D: Comparing medication dosages and outcomes

explanation: You've got this! Qualitative research is all about exploring real-life experiences, feelings, and the personal meanings people attach to health events, rather than just crunching numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: When would a nurse researcher choose a qualitative design?

options.A: To test a specific drug dosage on a group of people
options.B: To prove cause and effect using large numerical samples
options.C: To quickly measure blood pressure across a large population
options.D: To explore the emotional details of a patient's illness

explanation: Great thinking! We use qualitative designs when we want rich, descriptive stories about human experiences instead of cold numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h1)

question: What does a constructivist view assume about reality in qualitative research?

options.A: Reality is identical for every person with the same illness
options.B: Reality is a fixed physical truth that can be measured
options.C: Reality is subjective and shaped by individual experiences
options.D: Reality is determined strictly by laboratory blood tests

explanation: Spot on! Constructivism teaches that people build their own understanding of reality based on their unique lived experiences and daily interactions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: How does a researcher's philosophical viewpoint shape a qualitative study?

options.A: It determines the precise blood tests to perform on patients
options.B: It ensures that all participants give identical survey answers
options.C: It guides how the researcher views and interprets participant experiences
options.D: It dictates the exact statistical software needed for data analysis

explanation: Think of a paradigm as a pair of glasses—it shapes the researcher's entire approach to understanding and making sense of what people share. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which qualitative approach specifically focuses on exploring the lived experience of a concept?

options.A: Ethnography
options.B: Phenomenology
options.C: Clinical trial
options.D: Grounded theory

explanation: You can remember this easily: Phenomenology looks at 'phenomena' or lived experiences to uncover what a specific human experience truly feels like. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: A nurse wants to study the shared daily habits and culture of nurses in a busy emergency room. Which research approach fits best?

options.A: Phenomenology
options.B: Grounded theory
options.C: Ethnography
options.D: Randomized controlled trial

explanation: Brilliant! Ethnography is like diving into a specific cultural or social group to understand their shared workplace habits and lifestyle. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the main goal of purposive sampling in qualitative studies?

options.A: Choosing people randomly from a large national census list
options.B: Ensuring every person in the hospital has an equal chance to join
options.C: Selecting participants who have direct experience with the topic
options.D: Finding participants who disagree with the researcher's hypothesis

explanation: Exactly! 'Purposive' means on purpose—you pick people who actually lived the experience so they can give you the best information. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: What does 'data saturation' mean during qualitative interviews?

options.A: All participants have completed their medical treatments
options.B: The researcher has run out of financial funding for the study
options.C: The audio recording devices have stopped working properly
options.D: No new information or themes are emerging from interviews

explanation: Think of a sponge that is fully soaked. Saturation means you've heard it all; conducting more interviews isn't bringing up anything new, so you can wrap up! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which data collection method involves a guided group discussion about a shared topic?

options.A: Closed questionnaire
options.B: Focus group
options.C: Random survey
options.D: Laboratory assay

explanation: Spot on! A focus group brings a small circle of people together to talk openly, letting the researcher watch how they share and bounce ideas off each other. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why do qualitative researchers love open-ended questions?

options.A: They make it easy to enter numbers directly into a computer
options.B: They prevent participants from talking about sensitive topics
options.C: They encourage participants to share detailed personal stories
options.D: They guarantee that every interview takes exactly five minutes

explanation: You got it! Open-ended questions give people the freedom to talk in their own words, giving you rich, colourful stories instead of a simple 'yes' or 'no'. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h5)

question: What term do qualitative researchers use instead of traditional statistical terms like validity and reliability?

options.A: Trustworthiness
options.B: Numeric accuracy
options.C: Precision testing
options.D: Generalizability

explanation: Well done! Because qualitative work deals with stories and feelings rather than numbers, we check its quality by looking at its 'trustworthiness'. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the purpose of 'member checking' in a qualitative study?

options.A: To verify that all participants hold valid nursing licenses
options.B: To ensure that every survey contains no missing numerical data
options.C: To check if participants have paid their hospital admission fees
options.D: To confirm with participants that the researcher's interpretations are accurate

explanation: Easy peasy! Member checking is like going back to your participants and saying, 'Did I capture your story right?' to make sure you didn't misrepresent them. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main result you look for in a qualitative thematic analysis?

options.A: A laboratory value chart for patient diagnostics
options.B: A bar graph showing demographic frequency counts
options.C: Overarching themes that capture the meaning of the data
options.D: A precise statistical correlation coefficient

explanation: You're doing great! Thematic analysis groups all the interview notes into big, meaningful themes that tell the core story of the research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why is reflexivity important when analyzing qualitative data?

options.A: It speeds up the computer software processing time for transcripts
options.B: It helps researchers recognize and manage their personal biases
options.C: It automatically checks the mathematical accuracy of survey results
options.D: It proves that the study can be generalized to every hospital

explanation: Brilliant! Reflexivity means the researcher checks their own ego and personal views at the door so their own opinions don't colour the participants' stories. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT an acceptable ethical practice in qualitative research?

options.A: Protecting participant confidentiality through data anonymization
options.B: Publishing participant real names and home addresses
options.C: Obtaining informed consent prior to starting interviews
options.D: Allowing participants to withdraw from the study at any time

explanation: You nailed it! Patient and participant privacy is sacred. We never publish real names or private home details in research reports. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h8)

question: Why do we need to be extra careful with ethics in qualitative nursing research?

options.A: Participants are required to undergo invasive surgical procedures
options.B: Studies always involve testing high-risk experimental drugs
options.C: Interviews often touch on deeply personal and emotional experiences
options.D: Researchers must share participant private medical charts publicly

explanation: Spot on! Because qualitative chats often dig into sensitive feelings and life struggles, protecting emotional safety and privacy is our top priority as nurses. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T5#GNS224_U1_T5_h8)

question: In nursing research, what do we mean by a 'paradigm'?

options.A: A legal document required before treating patients
options.B: A strict mathematical formula for calculating sample size
options.C: A basic viewpoint or lens that guides how a study is approached
options.D: A specific brand of medical equipment used in hospitals

explanation: Think of a paradigm as your overall viewpoint or lens. It simply shapes how a researcher looks at a problem and decides to study it! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for student nurses to understand research paradigms?

options.A: To evaluate published studies and choose proper evidence for care
options.B: To calculate exact medication dosages for surgical patients
options.C: To diagnose rare diseases using laboratory blood test results
options.D: To write hospital administration policies without clinical data

explanation: Knowing this helps you look at a research paper and figure out if the findings make sense and can actually help your patients on the ward. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the main focus of quantitative research?

options.A: Historical observation of ancient medical texts
options.B: Open-ended interviews about emotional trauma
options.C: Numerical measurement and statistical analysis
options.D: Detailed personal stories of patient suffering

explanation: Quantitative research is all about numbers, counting, and statistics. If you can measure it, it's quantitative! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which of these nursing examples uses a quantitative design?

options.A: Recording a journal of daily emotional struggles during grief counseling
options.B: Observing nurse-patient interactions during a busy ward handover
options.C: Measuring hourly blood sugar levels after giving a new insulin dose
options.D: Interviewing elderly patients about their childhood memories of illness

explanation: Tracking blood sugar gives you clear numbers that you can run statistics on—that is the classic sign of quantitative research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h2)

question: What kind of data do you mainly collect in qualitative research?

options.A: Words, text, and descriptions of human experiences
options.B: Statistical percentages of patient readmissions
options.C: Exact laboratory blood chemistry measurements
options.D: Precise numerical vital signs recorded hourly

explanation: While quantitative loves numbers, qualitative loves words! It looks at interview notes and stories to understand human experiences. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the main goal of using a qualitative approach in a nursing study?

options.A: To find the exact percentage of patients cured by a drug
options.B: To measure the physical strength recovery of post-op clients
options.C: To gain a deep understanding of lived human experiences
options.D: To prove a mathematical relationship between two variables

explanation: Qualitative research helps us walk in our patients' shoes and truly understand what they are going through emotionally. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the core belief behind quantitative research?

options.A: A single objective reality exists that can be measured
options.B: Reality is entirely subjective and changes for every person
options.C: Facts only matter if the patient agrees with the nurse
options.D: There is no truth, only personal opinions in healthcare

explanation: Quantitative research assumes there is a clear, measurable truth out there waiting to be discovered with the right tools. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: How do qualitative and quantitative approaches differ in their main goals?

options.A: Qualitative avoids human subjects while quantitative studies only animals
options.B: Qualitative uses statistical formulas while quantitative uses personal stories
options.C: Qualitative focuses on lab equipment while quantitative focuses on interviews
options.D: Qualitative seeks deep meaning while quantitative seeks prediction and control

explanation: Simply put: qualitative wants to understand the 'why' and 'how' of feelings, while quantitative wants to measure and test facts. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which tool is commonly used to collect data in a quantitative study?

options.A: Unstructured conversational interview notes
options.B: Audio recordings of open-ended storytelling
options.C: Personal diaries written by study participants
options.D: Standardized surveys and measuring instruments

explanation: Quantitative researchers love structured tools like questionnaires, blood pressure cuffs, and monitors to keep data consistent. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: A researcher wants to study how nurses feel about working night shifts by having open conversations. Which data collection method is best?

options.A: Numerical blood pressure screening
options.B: In-depth qualitative interviews
options.C: A rigid multiple-choice questionnaire
options.D: Laboratory biomarker blood testing

explanation: Open-ended interviews are fantastic because they let nurses express their true feelings in their own words. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary way data is analyzed in quantitative research?

options.A: Translating ancient languages into modern English
options.B: Drawing pictures of patient physical posture
