options.C: Statistical tests and mathematical formulas
options.D: Extracting common themes from interview transcripts

explanation: Because quantitative data is made of numbers, you use math and statistics to make sense of it all. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: How does qualitative data analysis differ from quantitative analysis?

options.A: Qualitative analysis looks for recurring themes in text rather than numbers
options.B: Qualitative analysis ignores patient words and focuses on lab values
options.C: Qualitative analysis uses computer software to run complex regressions
options.D: Qualitative analysis requires strict mathematical proof of significance

explanation: Instead of crunching numbers, qualitative researchers read through text to find common patterns and themes in what people said. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which terms are used to evaluate the quality of a quantitative study?

options.A: Subjectivity and intuition
options.B: Credibility and transferability
options.C: Flexibility and emotion
options.D: Validity and reliability

explanation: Remember: quantitative studies live and die by validity (does it measure what it should?) and reliability (is it consistent?). [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: Why don't we use traditional validity and reliability tests in qualitative research?

options.A: Computers cannot calculate statistics on words the same way they do numbers
options.B: Qualitative researchers do not care if their findings are accurate or true
options.C: Human experiences are subjective and cannot be measured with rigid consistency
options.D: Ethics boards forbid researchers from testing qualitative data for errors

explanation: Human feelings and experiences change and cannot be put into a rigid numerical box, so qualitative research uses different checks for quality. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h7)

question: When should a nurse researcher pick a qualitative design over a quantitative one?

options.A: When testing if a new medication lowers blood pressure faster
options.B: When exploring the personal meaning and lived experience of a condition
options.C: When measuring the exact hospital readmission rate over a year
options.D: When calculating the average cost of surgical supplies per patient

explanation: Choose qualitative when you want to dive deep into personal stories, coping styles, and human emotions. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h8)

question: Which of these research questions is best answered with a quantitative design?

options.A: What is it like for a young mother to receive a diagnosis of breast cancer?
options.B: How do nurses emotionally experience the loss of a long-term patient?
options.C: Does a pre-operative education video reduce post-operative pain scores?
options.D: What meaning do elderly patients give to living in a nursing home?

explanation: Comparing pain scores before and after an intervention involves numbers and testing a hypothesis, which calls for quantitative research. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T6#GNS224_U1_T6_h8)

question: What is the main goal of experimental research design in healthcare?

options.A: To gather opinions from hospital staff
options.B: To observe patients without any interference
options.C: To describe the daily routine of a ward
options.D: To prove cause-and-effect relationships

explanation: Experiments are specifically built to show whether a specific action causes a specific result by actively changing one variable and measuring the outcome. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers use experimental designs instead of simple observation?

options.A: Observation cannot control outside factors that might skew results
options.B: Experiments are much easier to perform on busy wards
options.C: Patients prefer being in experimental groups
options.D: Observation takes too much money and time

explanation: Active control in experiments lets researchers rule out other explanations for patient recovery or change, giving much stronger proof than just watching patients. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h1)

question: What are the three core elements of a true experimental study?

options.A: Blinding, placebo, and sampling
options.B: Observation, interview, and survey
options.C: Manipulation, control, and randomization
options.D: Hypothesis, analysis, and conclusion

explanation: These three pillars separate true experiments from all other types of research by minimizing bias and proving causality. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: Why is randomization so important when assigning patients to study groups?

options.A: It gives every participant an equal chance of ending up in any group
options.B: It ensures that only the oldest patients get the new treatment
options.C: It makes the research paper shorter to write
options.D: It allows the nurse to choose which patient needs the therapy most

explanation: Randomization spreads patient differences evenly across groups, preventing researcher bias from messing up the final results. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which design offers the highest level of evidence by using all three core elements?

options.A: True experimental design
options.B: Quasi-experimental design
options.C: Pre-experimental design
options.D: Descriptive survey design

explanation: True experiments use manipulation, control, and randomization together, making their findings the most trustworthy for clinical guidelines. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: When is a nurse researcher most likely to choose a quasi-experimental design instead of a true experiment?

options.A: When the nurse wants to avoid doing any data analysis
options.B: When all patients must receive the exact same treatment
options.C: When random assignment of patients is impossible or unethical
options.D: When there is no budget to buy any research equipment

explanation: Clinical realities often prevent random assignment, such as studying existing groups like patients on two different hospital floors, forcing researchers to use quasi-methods. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the term for the outcome that a nurse researcher measures in an experiment?

options.A: Randomized variable
options.B: Dependent variable
options.C: Extraneous variable
options.D: Independent variable

explanation: The dependent variable depends on the intervention; it is the final health measurement or result you are recording. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: A nurse tests a new pain medication and measures the patient's reported pain score. What represents the independent variable?

options.A: The reported pain score
options.B: The new pain medication
options.C: The patient's age
options.D: The hospital noise level

explanation: The medication is what the researcher changes or gives to the patient, making it the independent variable (the cause). [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h4)

question: What does internal validity measure in an experimental study?

options.A: Whether the study can be used in every hospital worldwide
options.B: How many nurses were hired to assist with data collection
options.C: Whether the treatment truly caused the observed outcome
options.D: How fast the patients answered the survey questions

explanation: Internal validity checks if outside factors ruined the experiment, ensuring the intervention itself made the difference. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a good way to protect external validity in clinical research?

options.A: Testing patients only in a hidden laboratory with strict artificial rules
options.B: Conducting the study across multiple different hospitals
options.C: Including patients of various ages and backgrounds
options.D: Using a sample of participants that represents the real patient population

explanation: Overly artificial lab settings make it hard to apply the findings to normal, everyday clinical nursing practice, hurting external validity. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h5)

question: What must a nurse researcher obtain before starting any experiment involving human subjects?

options.A: A grant from a pharmaceutical company
options.B: Ethical approval from a review board
options.C: Approval from local newspaper reporters
options.D: Permission to buy new uniforms

explanation: Patient safety and rights must be protected, so an ethics committee must review and approve the study plan first. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why do researchers measure participants before and after giving an intervention?

options.A: To measure the exact change caused by the treatment
options.B: To give patients something to do while waiting
options.C: To fill up extra space in the final research report
options.D: To prove that all patients had identical health scores

explanation: Baseline measurements show where the patient started, letting researchers calculate the exact difference the intervention made. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h6)

question: What right does every participant have during a clinical research experiment?

options.A: To change the research questions whenever they want
options.B: To receive free lifetime medical care after the study
options.C: To choose which group they want to be placed in
options.D: To withdraw from the study at any time without penalty

explanation: Participation is completely voluntary, and patients can quit whenever they choose without affecting their regular hospital treatment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h7)

question: How do researchers ethically manage control groups when testing a new treatment?

options.A: By making sure the control group pays for their own hospital stay
options.B: By hiding the true purpose of the study from the hospital staff
options.C: By refusing to give any care at all to the control group
options.D: By giving the control group standard nursing care instead of nothing

explanation: Providing standard care ensures patients in the control group are not neglected or harmed while still allowing comparison against the new intervention. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is a major limitation of experimental research in busy hospitals?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for clinical judgment
options.B: It requires patients to stay in the hospital for years
options.C: It can be artificial and difficult to run in chaotic wards
options.D: It is always too cheap to get any meaningful results

explanation: The strict controls needed for experiments can clash with the messy reality of everyday hospital nursing routines. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h8)

question: A nurse manager wants to use experimental research to improve wound care on the surgical ward. What is the best reason to rely on this type of evidence?

options.A: It guarantees that patients will never develop an infection
options.B: It requires zero effort from the nursing staff on duty
options.C: It provides solid proof of which dressing heals wounds the fastest
options.D: It takes less time to read than a short textbook chapter

explanation: Solid causal evidence helps the nurse manager select patient care methods that are scientifically proven to work best. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T7#GNS224_U1_T7_h8)

question: What is the main thing that makes a research study 'non-experimental'?

options.A: The researcher does not manipulate the independent variable.
options.B: Random assignment is used for every participant.
options.C: A new treatment is tested against a placebo.
options.D: The study takes place only in a laboratory setting.

explanation: You've got this! In non-experimental studies, we simply watch and record things as they happen naturally, without changing or meddling with anything ourselves. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h1)

question: When would a nurse researcher decide to use a non-experimental design?

options.A: When ethical reasons prevent assigning patients to a harmful exposure
options.B: When proving that a specific nursing intervention directly causes a cure
options.C: When testing the exact dosage of a brand new surgical medication
options.D: When controlling every environmental factor in a hospital room

explanation: Spot on! Sometimes it is just plain wrong or unethical to expose people to risk on purpose (like smoking or harmful substances), so we use non-experimental designs to study them safely. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the main goal of a descriptive research design?

options.A: To accurately document characteristics of a population or situation
options.B: To test the effectiveness of a new surgical procedure
options.C: To prove that variable A causes a change in variable B
options.D: To compare two different patient groups after an intervention

explanation: Great job! Descriptive studies are all about painting a clear picture of what is going on right now, without needing to dig into the 'why' or 'how'. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h2)

question: A nurse wants to find out the percentage of pregnant women at a clinic who sleep less than five hours a night. Which design fits best?

options.A: Experimental design
options.B: Randomized controlled trial
options.C: Ex post facto design
options.D: Descriptive design

explanation: Brilliant! When you are just counting or checking the frequency of a habit or symptom in a group without testing a new drug or treatment, you are doing a descriptive study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h2)

question: What does a negative correlation mean between two variables?

options.A: Both variables decrease at the exact same time.
options.B: There is no relationship whatsoever between the variables.
options.C: The data collected by the researcher is invalid.
options.D: As one variable increases, the other variable decreases.

explanation: You're doing great! Think of it like a seesaw: when one thing goes up (like daily exercise), the other thing goes down (like resting blood pressure). That is a negative correlation! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h3)

question: A study shows that patients with higher anxiety report higher pain levels. Why can the researcher NOT claim that anxiety causes the pain?

options.A: Because anxiety is an experimental variable
options.B: Because pain cannot be measured using numerical scales
options.C: Because the sample size was likely too small to matter
options.D: Because correlational designs do not test cause and effect

explanation: Spot on! Finding a connection between two things just shows they move together; it doesn't prove one actually caused the other. Correlation is not causation! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h3)

question: What does the term 'ex post facto' mean?

options.A: Before the intervention
options.B: Randomly assigned
options.C: During the experiment
options.D: After the fact

explanation: Easy peasy! 'Ex post facto' simply means 'after the fact'. The event has already happened, and we are looking backward to figure out what might have caused it. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h4)

question: A researcher compares lung function in patients who developed chronic bronchitis against those who did not, looking back at their past smoking habits. Which design is this?

options.A: Cross-sectional design
options.B: Ex post facto design
options.C: True experimental design
options.D: Descriptive survey design

explanation: Well done! Because the health condition already happened and the researcher is digging into past history, it is an ex post facto (after the fact) study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which type of study collects data at just one single point in time?

options.A: Longitudinal study
options.B: Experimental trial
options.C: Cross-sectional study
options.D: Prospective cohort study

explanation: You've got this! A cross-sectional study is like taking a quick photograph—it gathers all the data from people at one specific moment. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is a major challenge when conducting a longitudinal study in nursing research?

options.A: Higher risk of manipulating the independent variable by accident
options.B: Inability to ever observe changes over time
options.C: Participants dropping out over time, leading to missing data
options.D: Results are always available immediately within days

explanation: Spot on! Following people for months or years is tough because participants sometimes move away, lose interest, or drop out, which researchers call attrition. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which of the following is a major limitation of non-experimental research?

options.A: Excessive control over the natural hospital environment
options.B: Impossibility of using statistical analysis
options.C: Unethical manipulation of patient treatment plans
options.D: Inability to definitively establish cause and effect

explanation: Great thinking! Because we aren't controlling every single outside factor or changing variables on purpose, we can't say for sure that one thing caused another. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why do non-experimental studies often have high ecological validity?

options.A: They use randomized blinding for all clinical procedures.
options.B: They take place inside strictly controlled laboratory rooms.
options.C: They observe people in their normal, everyday environments.
options.D: They completely eliminate all possible human errors.

explanation: Wonderful job! Since people are being watched in their natural settings rather than a strict lab, the findings reflect real life much better! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T8#GNS224_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the main goal of a descriptive research design?

options.A: To prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship between two treatments
options.B: To accurately describe a situation or population without changing variables
options.C: To test a new medical drug against a standard placebo
options.D: To manipulate patient routines and measure the physical outcome

explanation: Think of descriptive research like taking a clear photograph: you are just capturing things exactly as they are in real life without meddling or changing anything. Great job! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why must a nurse researcher use a descriptive design before starting an experimental trial?

options.A: Because descriptive data helps establish basic baseline knowledge about a problem
options.B: Because ethical boards legally forbid any nursing experiments without surveys
options.C: Because descriptive designs are the only way to get funding from hospitals
options.D: Because experiments always fail if they do not include a questionnaire

explanation: You cannot fix a problem if you don't first understand it! Descriptive work gives us that essential starting picture before we try out new treatments. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which feature is always true about a descriptive research study?

options.A: The researcher does not manipulate any variables
options.B: The study must take place inside a sterile laboratory
options.C: Only one person is observed at a time
options.D: Patients receive an experimental medicine

explanation: In descriptive studies, researchers take a hands-off approach. They observe and record without altering or tampering with anything. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h2)

question: What role do descriptive studies play in nursing science?

options.A: They supply baseline facts that point toward areas needing clinical investigation
options.B: They replace clinical trials by proving which drugs cure diseases
options.C: They force patients to alter their daily health habits for better outcomes
options.D: They eliminate all errors found in previous medical journals

explanation: Descriptive studies act like our radar—they highlight where health issues lie, guiding nurses on what needs closer study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the main characteristic of a cross-sectional descriptive study?

options.A: The researcher changes the patient's diet plan
options.B: Data is collected at one specific point in time
options.C: Only one patient is ever studied at a time
options.D: Participants are followed continuously for many years

explanation: Think of a cross-sectional study as a quick snapshot—it gathers information from a group at one single moment, with no long-term follow-up. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h3)

question: A nursing team wants to track how post-surgery mobility changes in elderly patients over the course of one year. Which design fits best?

options.A: Case study
options.B: Longitudinal study
options.C: Cross-sectional study
options.D: Laboratory experiment

explanation: When you want to watch patients grow, heal, or change over a long period (like a year), a longitudinal study is your go-to choice! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which tool is most frequently used to gather opinions from large groups in descriptive research?

options.A: Laboratory blood cultures
options.B: Surgical biopsy procedures
options.C: Surveys and questionnaires
options.D: Randomized drug trials

explanation: When you need to hear from many people quickly, questionnaires and surveys are the easiest and most practical tools to use. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h4)

question: A nurse researcher wants to study patient hygiene habits in a ward without changing their routine. What is the most suitable data collection approach?

options.A: A laboratory test
options.B: A clinical drug trial
options.C: Surgical intervention
options.D: Direct observation

explanation: To see how people naturally behave without them putting on an act, direct observation in their real environment works best. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h4)

question: What must be obtained before starting data collection with human participants in a study?

options.A: A commercial sponsor
options.B: Surgical clearance
options.C: A patent for a new drug
options.D: Ethical approval

explanation: Patient safety and rights always come first. Ethical approval ensures your study is safe and respects human dignity. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why is proper sampling important when conducting a descriptive survey in a hospital?

options.A: It guarantees that every single patient in the country will be cured
options.B: It removes the need to analyze numerical data at the end
options.C: It stops patients from answering survey questions incorrectly
options.D: It ensures the selected group accurately reflects the entire patient population

explanation: Good sampling means the few people you study are a true mini-version of the whole group, making your findings reliable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which of the following is an example of a descriptive statistic?

options.A: A surgical success prediction model
options.B: The exact biological cause of a virus mutation
options.C: A proven cure rate for a genetic disorder
options.D: Percentage of patients with high blood pressure

explanation: Numbers like percentages, averages, and counts are classic descriptive statistics that simply summarize what is happening in the data. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a common error when interpreting results from a descriptive study?

options.A: Using percentages to explain how many participants answered a survey
options.B: Concluding that one variable caused another simply because they occurred together
options.C: Creating a bar chart to display age groups in the sample
options.D: Comparing current findings with past published nursing literature

explanation: Just because two things happen at the same time doesn't mean one caused the other! Descriptive studies show connections, not direct causes. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a major limitation of descriptive research designs?

options.A: They require complex laboratory machinery
options.B: They cannot use questionnaires or interviews
options.C: They are too expensive for ordinary nursing students
options.D: They cannot prove cause-and-effect relationships

explanation: Because descriptive studies don't involve testing or experiments, they can only tell you what is happening, not why it is strictly causing something else. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of descriptive research?

options.A: Generating useful baseline data for future studies
options.B: Providing a clear picture of health habits in a community
options.C: Proving definitively which nursing intervention cures chronic illness
options.D: Being relatively fast and cost-effective to carry out

explanation: Descriptive research is great for painting a picture or saving time and money, but proving a cure requires heavy-duty experimental trials! [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h7)

question: How can a nurse manager use descriptive research on patient admission rates?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any further hospital documentation
options.B: To plan adequate staffing levels and shift rosters for busy periods
options.C: To test a new surgical procedure on incoming emergency patients
options.D: To prove that nurses cause patient illnesses during night shifts

explanation: Knowing peak admission times helps nurse managers schedule enough hands on deck so the ward runs smoothly and patients get great care. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h8)

question: A community health nurse conducts a survey to find out why mothers in a village do not bring children for immunization. What is the practical value of this study?

options.A: It guides the creation of a targeted local health education program
options.B: It forces every parent to pay a fine for missed immunizations
options.C: It proves that vaccines cure all known infectious diseases instantly
options.D: It replaces the need to administer vaccines in the clinic

explanation: By finding out the exact reasons for vaccine hesitancy, the nurse can design a friendly, localized outreach program that really helps the community. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T9#GNS224_U1_T9_h8)

question: What is the primary role of research data in nursing?

options.A: Complicating routine patient documentation tasks
options.B: Replacing the clinical judgment of experienced nurses
options.C: Reducing the total number of required hospital staff
options.D: Providing a foundation for evidence-based practice

explanation: Research data gives nurses the solid proof needed to choose the safest, most effective care methods. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h1)

question: How do everyday nursing activities relate to research data?

options.A: Routine documentation and vital sign monitoring actively generate data
options.B: Clinical tasks are completely separate from any form of data collection
options.C: Nurses only encounter research data when publishing academic books
options.D: Research data is only collected by doctors in specialized laboratories

explanation: Every time a nurse records patient signs or care outcomes, they are contributing to the pool of clinical research data. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which of the following is a clear example of quantitative data?

options.A: An interview transcript about coping with chronic illness
options.B: A detailed journal entry about living with heart failure
options.C: A patient's blood pressure reading of 120/80 mmHg
options.D: A narrative description of a nurse's shift experience

explanation: Quantitative data always involves numbers and measurements, such as blood pressure values. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h2)

question: What kind of information does qualitative data primarily capture?

options.A: Standardized monitoring device readouts and scores
options.B: Exact physical weights and chemical lab values
options.C: Precise mathematical frequencies and statistical averages
options.D: Human experiences, feelings, and descriptive narratives

explanation: Qualitative data focuses on words and stories that explain what a healthcare experience feels like to a patient. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h2)

question: What makes ratio data special compared to other levels of measurement?

options.A: Ratio data lacks any mathematical ordering
options.B: Ratio data can only be used for categorical groups
options.C: Ratio data has uneven spacing between values
options.D: Ratio data has a true, absolute zero point

explanation: You've got this! Ratio levels feature a true zero where zero means none of the item exists at all—like having zero milliliters of urine output. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h3)

question: A nurse classifies patient satisfaction scores as 'poor', 'fair', or 'good'. Which level of measurement is this?

options.A: Nominal
options.B: Ordinal
options.C: Ratio
options.D: Interval

explanation: Satisfaction grades have a logical order from poor to good, making them ordinal data, though the distance between the grades is not mathematically fixed. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the main advantage of using secondary data in nursing research?

options.A: It saves time and resources because someone else already collected it
options.B: It gives the researcher total control over how questions are asked
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any statistical analysis
options.D: It guarantees that there will be zero errors in the dataset

explanation: Secondary data lets researchers study large topics quickly using existing records without setting up new data collection projects. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following describes a primary data collection method?

options.A: Reading a published textbook summary of historical mortality rates
options.B: Interviewing patients directly after surgery for a new study
options.C: Downloading a public census file from a government website
options.D: Extracting anonymized blood pressure logs from old hospital archives

explanation: Primary data is gathered firsthand by the researcher specifically to answer their own current research question. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h4)

question: In a nursing research study, what does the independent variable stand for?

options.A: An unexpected error that ruins the study measurements
options.B: A constant baseline factor that never changes or varies
options.C: The final measured outcome that changes as a result
options.D: The presumed cause or experimental intervention being tested

explanation: Think of the independent variable as the treatment or action the nurse researcher introduces to see what effect it has! [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h5)

question: A researcher studies whether a new walking program lowers blood pressure in elderly patients. What is the dependent variable?

options.A: Blood pressure level
options.B: The researcher conducting the study
options.C: The walking program
options.D: The age of the elderly patients

explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome being measured, which in this case is the patient's blood pressure responding to the exercise. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why is data screening necessary before conducting statistical analysis?

options.A: To catch entry errors and missing values that could distort results
options.B: To make the dataset large enough for international publication
options.C: To eliminate the need for any ethical approval board review
options.D: To change patient outcomes so the research hypothesis is proven right

explanation: Screening ensures that impossible entries or typos do not ruin the accuracy of the final research findings. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: During data screening, which of these findings is clearly wrong and needs immediate fixing?

options.A: A slight variation in the average age of study volunteers
options.B: A missing response on a secondary satisfaction survey question
options.C: A patient heart rate recorded as 1,200 beats per minute
options.D: A normal demographic spread of male and female participants

explanation: Great catch! A human heart rate of 1,200 beats per minute is physically impossible and points to a simple data entry typo. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of data organization in nursing research?

options.A: To publish findings without peer review
options.B: To eliminate the need for statistical testing
options.C: To increase the total number of study participants
options.D: To structure raw information so it can be analyzed

explanation: Organizing raw data transforms messy notes and numbers into a structured format that allows researchers to look for patterns and run accurate analysis. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h1)

question: In a standard research dataset, what does each row typically represent?

options.A: A summary of missing values
options.B: The final statistical conclusion
options.C: A different measurement scale
options.D: A single participant or subject

explanation: Standard datasets are arranged so that each horizontal row corresponds to one individual participant, while the vertical columns represent the variables measured. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h1)

question: Blood type classification represents which type of measurement scale?

options.A: Nominal scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Ordinal scale
options.D: Ratio scale

explanation: Nominal scales deal with named categories that do not have any mathematical order or ranking, such as blood types. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h2)

question: A nurse records a patient's exact weight in kilograms. What type of measurement scale is this?

options.A: Nominal scale
options.B: Interval scale
options.C: Ordinal scale
options.D: Ratio scale

explanation: Weight is measured on a ratio scale because it has equal intervals and a true zero point where zero kilograms means an absolute absence of weight. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the process of assigning numbers to qualitative categories called?

options.A: Data coding
options.B: Data graphing
options.C: Data cleaning
options.D: Data scaling

explanation: Coding is the translation of descriptive categories into numerical codes to make computer entry and statistical analysis straightforward. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why is data cleaning an essential step before running statistical tests?

options.A: It eliminates the need to obtain ethical clearance
options.B: It ensures all participants completed the survey
options.C: It catches entry errors and impossible values that distort results
options.D: It automatically converts nominal data into ratio data

explanation: Cleaning data allows researchers to spot typos and unrealistic entries, ensuring the final statistical findings reflect true clinical observations. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h3)

question: What does the frequency column in a distribution table tell a researcher?

options.A: The total number of missing patient files
options.B: The mathematical average of the dataset
options.C: How many times a specific value occurs
options.D: The exact date the data was collected

explanation: Frequency simply counts the number of times a particular score, category, or observation appears in the dataset. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is the main advantage of using a relative frequency column instead of just raw counts?

options.A: It shows proportions and percentages for easy comparison
options.B: It automatically changes ordinal data into interval data
options.C: It prevents outliers from appearing in the table
options.D: It corrects any typos made during data entry

explanation: Relative frequency turns raw counts into percentages, making it much easier to compare groups of different sizes. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why are there spaces between the bars in a standard bar chart?

options.A: To show that the categories are separate and distinct
options.B: To indicate that numerical data is continuous
options.C: To make room for writing long patient names
options.D: To represent missing values in the dataset

explanation: Bar charts display categorical data where each category stands alone, so spaces between bars visually separate them. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h5)

question: A nurse wants to show the percentage breakdown of patient satisfaction ratings across four distinct wards. Which graph is most appropriate?

options.A: Pie chart
options.B: Scatter plot
options.C: Histogram
options.D: Line graph

explanation: Pie charts are ideal for displaying percentage shares of a whole, such as how different wards share out total satisfaction categories. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a key visual difference between a bar chart and a histogram?

options.A: Histograms have touching bars because data is continuous
options.B: Histograms are only used for nominal data categories
options.C: Bar charts display changes over time on the vertical axis
options.D: Bar charts use circles instead of rectangular bars

explanation: Because histograms represent continuous numerical ranges, their bars touch each other to show that the scale flows without gaps. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h6)

question: A ward nurse needs to visually track a post-operative patient's temperature fluctuations every two hours over a full day. Which graph should the nurse choose?

options.A: Bar chart
options.B: Line graph
options.C: Nominal table
options.D: Pie chart

explanation: Line graphs are designed to show trends and changes in numerical measurements over continuous intervals like time. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is an outlier in a research dataset?

options.A: A missing patient file that was never collected
options.B: A category label used for nominal variables
options.C: The exact mathematical average of a frequency table
options.D: An extreme value that sits far away from other data points

explanation: Outliers are data entries that are unusually high or low compared to the vast majority of the observations in the dataset. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why should a nurse researcher investigate an outlier rather than deleting it immediately?

options.A: Outliers always improve the accuracy of statistical tests
options.B: It proves that the measurement scale was ordinal
options.C: Deleting data is illegal in all health research
options.D: It might represent a genuine, important clinical finding

explanation: An extreme value might look like an error at first glance, but it could actually reflect a real, critical clinical event that deserves attention. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h7)

question: What does de-identifying a dataset involve?

options.A: Deleting all outliers and missing values from the study
options.B: Removing direct identifiers like patient names and hospital numbers
options.C: Publishing raw patient records in public journals
options.D: Converting all numerical data into categorical scales

explanation: De-identification protects patient privacy by stripping away personal details and replacing them with anonymous tracking numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h8)

question: Why is ethical data management particularly critical in nursing research?

options.A: Because it prevents frequency tables from having errors
options.B: Because computers cannot process named data without codes
options.C: Because nursing data involves sensitive personal health information
options.D: Because ethical clearance replaces the need for data cleaning

explanation: Healthcare records are deeply private, and nurses have an ethical duty to safeguard patient confidentiality throughout every step of data organization. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T2#GNS224_U2_T2_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of data interpretation in nursing research?

options.A: To hide negative results from hospital administrators and staff
options.B: To collect as many patient surveys as possible without analysis
options.C: To make sure every research study costs less money to run
options.D: To turn raw research findings into meaningful conclusions for care

explanation: Data interpretation translates raw numbers and notes into clear findings that nurses can use to improve patient care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is data interpretation so important before a hospital changes its nursing guidelines?

options.A: It ensures new guidelines are based on proof rather than random chance
options.B: It proves that nurses do not need to attend extra training workshops
options.C: It stops doctors from making independent decisions about medication
options.D: It guarantees that every single patient in the hospital gets cured

explanation: Interpreting data carefully helps researchers confirm that an intervention actually worked, preventing hospitals from adopting unproven ideas. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h1)

question: What must happen to qualitative data, like recorded patient interviews, before analysis?

options.A: They must be transcribed word-for-word into written text
options.B: They must be translated into three different foreign languages
options.C: They must be deleted immediately to protect hospital files
options.D: They must be converted entirely into bar charts and graphs

explanation: Audio recordings of interviews need to be written out as text transcripts so researchers can read, code, and analyze the themes. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h2)

question: A researcher spots a few strange blood pressure numbers that look like typos in the database. What is the best first step?

options.A: Ignore the mistakes and run the statistical analysis anyway
options.B: Change the numbers randomly to fit the average reading
options.C: Check the original paper records to verify the correct entry
options.D: Delete all the patient records so they do not ruin the study

explanation: Data cleaning means checking suspicious entries against original source documents rather than guessing or deleting data carelessly. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which descriptive statistic represents the exact middle value of a dataset?

options.A: Mode
options.B: Median
options.C: Mean
options.D: Standard deviation

explanation: The median splits the dataset directly in half, with fifty percent of the values above it and fifty percent below. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why do researchers often prefer the median over the mean when looking at how long patients stay in the hospital?

options.A: The median is much harder to calculate using modern computer software
options.B: Length of stay can only be measured in whole numbers of days
options.C: A few patients staying an unusually long time can distort the average
options.D: Hospital administrators refuse to look at mathematical averages

explanation: Extreme outliers, like a patient staying 100 days, pull the mean way up, whereas the median stays stable and shows the typical experience. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h3)

question: What does a p-value of less than 0.05 generally tell us in a research study?

options.A: The results are statistically significant and unlikely to be a fluke
options.B: The researchers made a major calculation error in their software
options.C: The study had five percent more patients drop out than expected
options.D: The treatment plan worked for exactly five percent of the patients

explanation: A p-value below 0.05 shows strong evidence that the result didn't just happen by pure coincidence! [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why must a nurse be careful not to confuse statistical significance with real clinical usefulness?

options.A: Clinical importance only matters if the p-value is exactly equal to zero
options.B: A tiny change in numbers can reach statistical significance in a huge study without helping patients much
options.C: Statistical programs always hide the real health outcomes from the nursing staff
options.D: Statistical significance is completely made up and has no place in modern hospital wards

explanation: If a study is massive, even a tiny, unimportant number change can look 'statistically significant' even if patients don't feel any real health benefit. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the primary focus of qualitative data analysis in healthcare research?

options.A: Measuring the exact blood pressure drop after medication
options.B: Counting how many hospital beds are filled each night
options.C: Calculating exact drug dosages and patient body weights
options.D: Exploring human experiences, feelings, and recurring themes

explanation: Qualitative research focuses on understanding the subjective experiences and perspectives of participants rather than measuring quantities. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do researchers usually find common themes in qualitative interview notes?

options.A: By selecting only the longest interview and ignoring all the others
options.B: By throwing away any interview answer that does not match their personal opinion
options.C: By reading through the text repeatedly to identify patterns and grouping similar ideas
options.D: By feeding every sentence into a calculator to find the mathematical mean

explanation: Thematic analysis takes patience: researchers read the text over and over to spot patterns and group similar ideas together. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h5)

question: What does it mean to put research results into 'context'?

options.A: Translating the research report into three different languages
options.B: Comparing new study findings with past literature and clinical realities
options.C: Destroying old textbooks so staff only read the newest articles
options.D: Increasing the hospital budget to match the research costs

explanation: Contextualization just means looking at how new findings fit alongside existing science and whether they make sense on a busy ward. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h6)

question: A clinic nurse reads about a brilliant new wound care gadget, but her clinic lacks the budget and steady electricity to run it. What should she consider?

options.A: Whether the study findings fit the practical limitations of her local work environment
options.B: Whether she should resign from her job for not having enough equipment
options.C: Whether the researchers made a math error in their statistical calculations
options.D: Whether all wound care studies should be banned from medical journals

explanation: Local context matters greatly. A great gadget is useless if your clinic doesn't have the resources or steady power to support it! [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is a 'confounding factor' in healthcare research?

options.A: A hospital policy that requires nurses to wear protective uniforms
options.B: A type of patient interview question that cannot be transcribed
options.C: A hidden variable that can distort the true relationship between cause and effect
options.D: A mathematical mistake made when calculating the standard deviation

explanation: A confounder is a sneaky hidden factor that makes it look like a treatment caused a result when something else actually played a major role. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why is it important for a research paper to include a section about its own limitations?

options.A: It proves that the researchers spent a lot of money conducting the study
options.B: It ensures that other scientists never try to research that topic again
options.C: It shows honesty about potential flaws and stops readers from overgeneralizing conclusions
options.D: It gives the journal editors an excuse to reject the paper before publication

explanation: No study is 100% perfect. Admitting limitations helps other clinicians know where the findings might fall short so they don't overstate the results. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the ultimate goal of interpreting research data in nursing?

options.A: To help university professors publish more academic textbooks
options.B: To give hospital managers more paperwork to file away
options.C: To improve patient care and guide evidence-based clinical practice
options.D: To reduce the number of nurses working in hospital wards

explanation: At the end of the day, research data only matters if it helps us make patient care safer and better! [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h8)

question: Which of these is NOT a good quality for a clinical recommendation based on research data?

options.A: Being directly supported by the findings of the study
options.B: Being clear and easy for frontline nurses to understand
options.C: Being realistic about the equipment available in the clinic
options.D: Being completely unrealistic and impossible for staff to carry out

explanation: Good recommendations must be practical. If a guideline is impossible to carry out on a real ward, busy clinical staff will simply ignore it. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T3#GNS224_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is the main goal of presenting research results in nursing?

options.A: To show off complex mathematical calculations
options.B: To hide missing values and recording errors
options.C: To tell an honest and accurate story about the data
options.D: To prove that the hypothesis was always correct

explanation: The primary purpose of data presentation is to clearly and honestly communicate what the research findings reveal to other professionals. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why must researchers clean their data before presenting the results?

options.A: To convert all qualitative words into numbers
options.B: To ensure the study meets word count requirements
options.C: To prevent errors from distorting the final findings
options.D: To make the statistical analysis completely unnecessary

explanation: Checking for missing values and errors beforehand ensures that the data presentation reflects true clinical realities rather than mistakes. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h1)

question: When is a statistical table best used in a research report?

options.A: When replacing the narrative text entirely
options.B: When describing a single patient's emotional journey
options.C: When presenting large amounts of precise numerical data
options.D: When showing general trends and patterns over time

explanation: Tables excel at organizing large volumes of exact numbers so readers can easily locate specific values. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h2)

question: A researcher wants to show how blood pressure readings changed across four different clinic visits for a group of patients. Which format should they choose?

options.A: A graph
options.B: A qualitative interview transcript
options.C: A dense text paragraph
options.D: A demographic listing

explanation: Graphs are the best format for illustrating trends and changes across multiple time points, like clinic visits. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of table footnotes in a research paper?

options.A: To list the names of all the study participants
options.B: To provide a detailed biography of the researcher
options.C: To hide data that does not support the hypothesis
options.D: To define abbreviations and symbols used in the table

explanation: Footnotes explain abbreviations like SD or CI so readers can easily interpret the table elements. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h3)

question: How should numerical data inside a statistical table be aligned for easy reading?

options.A: Centered randomly
options.B: By the decimal point
options.C: To the far right margin
options.D: To the far left margin

explanation: Aligning numbers by their decimal points makes it much easier to compare values vertically. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why should the vertical axis on a bar chart usually start at zero?

options.A: To make all the bars look exactly the same height
options.B: To hide negative values from the reader
options.C: To prevent exaggerating small differences between groups
options.D: To ensure the chart fits onto a standard notebook page

explanation: Starting at zero maintains correct visual proportions so readers do not misinterpret minor changes as massive clinical differences. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which type of graph is best suited for showing continuous data tracked over time?

options.A: Scatter table
options.B: Line graph
options.C: Demographic matrix
options.D: Pie chart

explanation: Line graphs are specifically designed to illustrate trends and changes across sequential time points. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary building block used to present qualitative research findings?

options.A: Zero-baseline bar charts
options.B: Statistical p-values and correlations
options.C: Themes and direct participant quotes
options.D: Decimal-aligned numeric tables

explanation: Qualitative research focuses on human experiences, which are presented through organized themes and verbatim quotes rather than numbers. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why do qualitative researchers include direct quotes from participants in their results?

options.A: To let participants speak in their own voices and add authenticity
options.B: To replace the need for any written interpretation or analysis
options.C: To increase the total word count of the research report
options.D: To prove that every participant agreed with the researcher

explanation: Verbatim quotes provide direct evidence of the lived experiences, making the qualitative narrative believable and grounded in reality. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is selective reporting in research?

options.A: Using pseudonyms to protect the identity of study participants
options.B: Aligning numbers by their decimal points in a table
options.C: Highlighting only supportive data while hiding contradictory results
options.D: Choosing between a bar chart and a statistical table

explanation: Selective reporting is an unethical practice where researchers suppress unfavorable findings to present a biased picture. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT an ethical practice when presenting qualitative research results?

options.A: Revealing the real names of participants to give them credit
options.B: Reporting all findings honestly, even unexpected ones
options.C: Separating factual results from personal opinions
options.D: Using pseudonyms to protect participant confidentiality

explanation: Participant confidentiality is paramount; revealing real names without explicit consent breaches ethical research standards. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T4#GNS224_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of the discussion section in a research paper?

options.A: To detail the exact steps of the data collection process
options.B: To present raw statistical data without any interpretation
options.C: To list the demographic characteristics of the participants
options.D: To explain the meaning of the results and their implications

explanation: You've got this! The discussion section takes those dry numbers and explains what they actually mean for everyday nursing practice. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why shouldn't a researcher just repeat the results in the discussion section?

options.A: Results only show what happened, whereas the discussion explains why it matters
options.B: Statistical tables are too large to fit comfortably inside the discussion
options.C: Readers already memorized the numbers during the literature review
options.D: Journal editors charge extra fees for duplicating data in two sections

explanation: Great thinking! Just copying the numbers over doesn't help anyone. The discussion is where you bring the meaning to life. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h1)

question: How is the best way to kick off the discussion section?

options.A: By summarizing the primary findings in plain language
options.B: By proposing a brand new theory of human behavior
options.C: By listing every single p-value calculated in the study
options.D: By criticizing the work done by previous authors

explanation: Spot on! Starting with a clear, simple summary reminds your reader of the main scoop before you dive deep into what it all means. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h2)

question: When summarizing key results for a study on preventing pressure sores, what belongs right at the start?

options.A: Detailed instructions on how to use turning sheets
options.B: A complete list of every patient's medical history
options.C: Raw survey responses from all participating nurses
options.D: The main answer to the primary research question

explanation: You're crushing it! Always address the main question first so your reader immediately knows what the study found. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h2)

question: What should a nurse researcher do if their new results don't match older studies?

options.A: Hide the contradictory data so the paper gets published
options.B: Explore potential reasons for the differences in findings
options.C: Change the original hypothesis to match the old literature
options.D: Assume all previous researchers made mistakes in math

explanation: Exactly! Science grows when we look closely at *why* results differ—maybe times have changed, or the patient group is different. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why do we connect our new research findings back to older, published studies?

options.A: It proves that the current researcher is smarter than past authors
options.B: It is a strict legal requirement for copyright clearance
options.C: It shows whether the new results support or challenge existing knowledge
options.D: It ensures that no new statistical tests need to be run

explanation: Well done! Connecting new data to past work helps us see the bigger picture of how nursing knowledge builds over time. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the right move when a study throws a totally unexpected result your way?

options.A: Throw away the entire dataset and start the study over
options.B: Discuss them honestly and suggest potential reasons for the outcome
options.C: Blame the participants for failing to follow instructions properly
options.D: Pretend the unexpected data points do not exist in the report

explanation: You've got this! Honesty is everything in research. Surprising results often teach us the most valuable lessons. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h4)

question: If a pain-relief trial shows patients actually felt *more* distressed after the new method, what should the discussion do?

options.A: Conclude that the nursing profession should stop measuring pain entirely
options.B: Change the data labels so distress looks like pain relief
options.C: Examine what factors might have caused this surprising increase in distress
options.D: Publish the paper immediately without mentioning the pain scores

explanation: Spot on! We can't hide unexpected outcomes. Facing them head-on helps protect patients and improves future care. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h4)

question: If a small study of 5 patients shows a new positioning trick stops bedsores, what should the implications say?

options.A: Every hospital in the country must immediately adopt this exact positioning technique
options.B: The technique shows promise, but larger studies are needed before changing hospital policy
options.C: Research involving human subjects should be banned immediately
options.D: Patient positioning has no impact whatsoever on skin integrity

explanation: Brilliant! With a tiny group of patients, we stay hopeful and careful before rewriting hospital rules for everyone. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT something you should focus on when writing nursing practice implications?

options.A: Suggesting updates to bedside clinical nursing procedures
options.B: Calculating the personal financial bonuses for the lead researcher
options.C: Recommending changes to nursing school education programs
options.D: Highlighting how patient safety can be improved based on data

explanation: You nailed it! Nursing research is all about better patient care and safer practice—never about pocketing extra cash. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is it important for a researcher to list study limitations in the discussion?

options.A: To give critics an easy way to reject the paper from journals
options.B: To lengthen the article so it meets minimum word counts
options.C: To show transparency and acknowledge boundaries of the findings
options.D: To prove that the research methods used were completely flawless

explanation: Great job! Every study has weak spots. Being open about them shows you are a thoughtful, honest nurse researcher. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h6)

question: If a diet study relies entirely on patients writing down what they ate in a diary, what limitation should you mention?

options.A: Excessive use of expensive laboratory equipment
options.B: Too many blood samples taken from participants
options.C: Potential bias from self-reported data
options.D: Severe physical injuries caused by the diary

explanation: Spot on! People sometimes forget what they ate—or write down what they *wish* they ate. We have to keep that in mind! [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the main goal of giving recommendations for future research?

options.A: To give graduate students easy thesis topics they do not have to think about
options.B: To guide subsequent studies based on current gaps and unanswered questions
options.C: To prove that the current study answered every single question in nursing
options.D: To ensure the original researcher gets paid for all future grants

explanation: You've got this! No single study answers everything. Pointing out what's left to discover helps the next wave of researchers. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h7)

question: A study tests a stress-relief program for nurses in a busy city hospital. What is a great recommendation for future research?

options.A: Firing all city hospital nurses who reported high stress levels
options.B: Replacing human nurses with automated computer terminals
options.C: Testing if the same program works effectively in rural clinics
options.D: Stopping all future research on nurse mental health

explanation: Brilliant! Testing the same idea in a different setting helps us see if it works for nurses everywhere, not just in the city. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T5#GNS224_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a research proposal?

options.A: To summarize the final conclusions of a completed study
options.B: To publish patient case studies in a medical journal
options.C: To outline a planned study before collecting data
options.D: To evaluate the daily performance of hospital staff

explanation: A research proposal acts as a blueprint prepared before any investigation starts. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is writing a proposal considered a necessary step for nurse researchers?

options.A: It replaces the need for an official ethics committee review
options.B: It guarantees immediate funding from the government
options.C: It automatically cures the clinical problem being studied
options.D: It ensures the study plan is clear and feasible beforehand

explanation: Working through a proposal forces the researcher to organize their thoughts and check feasibility before spending resources. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the main reason why nurses conduct research and write proposals?

options.A: To increase the administrative workload of nurses
options.B: Improve patient care and clinical outcomes
options.C: Completely eliminate hospital budgets
options.D: To reduce the number of registered nurses needed

explanation: At the end of the day, everything we do in nursing research is about finding better ways to help our patients heal safely at the bedside. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h2)

question: A nurse wants to test a new turning schedule to prevent bedsores in her ward. What should she do first before trying it out on patients?

options.A: Discharge all patients currently at risk of bedsores
options.B: Ask patients to fund the new hospital mattresses
options.C: Immediately apply the schedule to all ward patients
options.D: Write a formal research proposal for review

explanation: Before introducing any new change or test on vulnerable patients, you must write a formal proposal and get proper approval. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which section of a proposal summarizes the entire document and is usually written last?

options.A: Budget
options.B: Reference list
options.C: Methodology
options.D: Abstract

explanation: The abstract is a short summary that gives readers a quick overview of the whole proposal. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the main job of the methodology section in a research proposal?

options.A: To list every book ever written on nursing
options.B: To praise previous researchers in the field
options.C: To prove that the researcher has a large budget
options.D: To explain how the study will be carried out

explanation: The methodology is your step-by-step game plan. It explains the exact tools, steps, and designs you will use to gather and check your data. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of a problem statement in a research proposal?

options.A: Convinces the reader that a specific issue requires study
options.B: Lists the exact financial cost of the research project
options.C: Provides a complete list of all hospital staff members
options.D: Summarizes the final results found after data collection

explanation: A problem statement points out the exact gap or trouble in current clinical practice that your research is going to help fix. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why do we need our research questions to be very clear and specific?

options.A: To confuse readers who are not nurses
options.B: To ensure the study collects relevant and measurable data
options.C: To prevent the ethics committee from reading the proposal
options.D: To make the proposal document as long as possible

explanation: Clear questions keep you on track so you don't end up collecting information you don't need! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why is a literature review so important when writing a proposal?

options.A: To criticize every nurse who worked before you
options.B: To fill up empty pages in the research document
options.C: To identify existing knowledge gaps on the topic
options.D: To gather personal opinions from hospital patients

explanation: Reviewing past studies shows you what has already been done and helps you find out what is still missing so your study adds real value. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h5)

question: How should past studies be presented in a good literature review?

options.A: A random list of book titles found in the library
options.B: Unchecked rumors heard around the hospital ward
options.C: Personal diary entries written by the researcher
options.D: A critical analysis and grouping of past studies by themes

explanation: Instead of just listing past papers one by one, you group them by themes and discuss what they mean together. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which research design focuses primarily on numbers, measurements, and statistical analysis?

options.A: Historical research
options.B: Qualitative research
options.C: Quantitative research
options.D: Biographical research

explanation: Quantitative research deals with measurable variables and numerical data. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why must a researcher carefully explain how they chose their participants (sample selection)?

options.A: To make the research budget look much smaller than it is
options.B: To hide the identities of the nurses working on the ward
options.C: So others understand who was studied and can judge if results are fair
options.D: To ensure that only wealthy patients take part in the study

explanation: Being transparent about your participants builds trust and shows everyone that your results are reliable and unbiased. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is compulsory before a patient takes part in a nursing research study?

options.A: A financial deposit
options.B: Informed consent
options.C: Hospital employment
options.D: A government passport

explanation: Patients must always be fully informed about the study and willingly agree to participate of their own free will. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why do research proposals have to be checked by an ethics committee?

options.A: To ensure human rights and patient safety are fully protected
options.B: To calculate the exact profit the hospital will make
options.C: To decide which nursing journal will publish the final paper
options.D: To check if the grammar and spelling are completely perfect

explanation: Ethics boards are there to watch out for patients, ensuring that no study causes harm and that everything is done morally. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which of the following is a good practice, and NOT a common mistake in research proposals?

options.A: Failing to plan proper ethical protections
options.B: Choosing a topic that is far too broad to manage
options.C: Relying heavily on outdated reference materials
options.D: Ensuring alignment between questions and methods

explanation: Making sure your research questions match your methods is a brilliant practice! The other options are classic pitfalls to avoid. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h8)

question: A student proposes to study 'every health issue affecting every patient in the country.' What is the main problem with this topic?

options.A: The methodology uses too many statistical tests
options.B: It focuses too much on ethical patient consent
options.C: It relies entirely on recent nursing journals
options.D: The scope is far too broad to be manageable

explanation: A good proposal needs a narrow, focused topic so you can actually finish it successfully without getting overwhelmed! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T1#GNS224_U3_T1_h8)

question: When writing a research proposal for a study you haven't done yet, what tense should you use?

options.A: Future tense
options.B: Conditional tense
options.C: Present tense
options.D: Past tense

explanation: Since the research hasn't happened yet, you're planning for what you *will* do. That means keeping everything in the future tense! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why do nurse researchers submit a proposal before starting any study?

options.A: To recruit patients for immediate bedside treatment
options.B: To replace standard hospital nursing policies
options.C: To secure formal approval and ensure safety
options.D: To publish final clinical results quickly

explanation: Ethics committees need to check your plan first to make sure your patients are fully protected from harm. Safety always comes first! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h1)

question: Where do the best nursing research ideas usually spark from?

options.A: Everyday clinical observations
options.B: Hospital financial statements
options.C: Government tax reports
options.D: Pharmaceutical marketing brochures

explanation: Think about things you notice right on the ward! The challenges and patterns you see during clinical rotations make the most meaningful research topics. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h2)

question: A student wants to study 'hospital stress'. Which option is a well-focused, realistic research topic?

options.A: Reviewing the history of global healthcare systems
options.B: Comparing the salaries of all hospital workers worldwide
options.C: Assessing night-shift burnout among intensive care unit nurses
options.D: Finding out why people get stressed in all buildings

explanation: Great research topics are narrow and specific! Focusing on a particular group (ICU nurses) and issue (night-shift burnout) makes your study much easier to manage. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h2)

question: How should information flow when you are writing your research background?

options.A: From personal opinions up to international laws
options.B: From future predictions back to ancient history
options.C: From broad global issues down to local problems
options.D: From rare individual cases up to general theories

explanation: Imagine a funnel! You start with the big picture worldwide, then narrow it down step-by-step until you reach your specific local hospital or ward. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is the main job of the 'statement of the problem' in your proposal?

options.A: To list the names of every nurse working on the ward
options.B: To summarize the final conclusions of the study
options.C: To highlight the exact gap or issue requiring research
options.D: To advertise new medical equipment to the hospital

explanation: The problem statement tells your reader: 'Here is what we don't know yet, and here is why our study needs to fix it!' [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h3)

question: Research objectives need to be clear and measurable. What kind of words should they always start with?

options.A: Pronouns
options.B: Action verbs
options.C: Prepositions
options.D: Adjectives

explanation: Always kick off your objectives with active words like 'to evaluate', 'to assess', or 'to compare' so everyone knows exactly what you plan to do. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h4)

question: In simple terms, what is a research hypothesis?

options.A: A tentative prediction about the study variables
options.B: A summary of financial costs for the project
options.C: A proven fact gathered from historical records
options.D: A list of equipment needed for data collection

explanation: A hypothesis is basically your educated guess about what you think your study will discover. You test it to see if you're right! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why do we spend time doing a thorough literature review?

options.A: Provides free medical supplies for the hospital ward
options.B: Preventing the repetition of already completed studies
options.C: Eliminates the need for a formal methodology section
options.D: Guarantees immediate funding from international donors

explanation: Checking existing literature makes sure you aren't reinventing the wheel. You want to build on past discoveries, not copy work that's already done! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which of these sources is the most trusted and reliable for an academic literature review?

options.A: Personal diary entries of patients
options.B: Anonymous social media posts
options.C: Peer-reviewed journal articles
options.D: Commercial product advertisements

explanation: Peer-reviewed articles have been checked and approved by other experts in healthcare, making them solid evidence for your study. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h5)

question: When is it best for a nurse researcher to choose a qualitative study design?

options.A: When measuring physical vital signs with a machine
options.B: When calculating exact drug dosages and blood levels
options.C: When comparing large statistical datasets of numbers
options.D: When exploring deep human experiences and meanings

explanation: Qualitative research is all about words, feelings, and personal stories. Use it when you want to understand *how* people feel or experience things. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h6)

question: A nurse wants to test if a new handwashing technique actually lowers ward infection rates. What study design fits best?

options.A: Historical biography
options.B: Qualitative phenomenology
options.C: Philosophical essay
options.D: Quantitative experimental

explanation: Because you are tracking numbers (infection rates) and testing an intervention, you need a quantitative experimental approach! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h6)

question: What do we call the complete group of people that a researcher is interested in studying?

options.A: Pilot cohort
options.B: Target population
options.C: Control group
options.D: Sample subset

explanation: The target population is the big group that shares the exact traits you want to investigate—like all nursing students in Nigeria, for instance! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h7)

question: How do you know if a data collection tool (like a questionnaire) is truly valid?

options.A: It accurately measures what it is intended to measure
options.B: It has been approved by the hospital accountant
options.C: It is extremely cheap to print and distribute
options.D: It takes less than two minutes for patients to finish

explanation: Validity just means your tool does the job it's supposed to do—it's actually testing the specific variable you care about. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h7)

question: What crucial step must a researcher complete with participants before collecting any data?

options.A: Medical insurance details
options.B: Employment contracts
options.C: Informed consent
options.D: Financial donations

explanation: Patients must always agree willingly to join your study after you explain what will happen. Getting informed consent is a non-negotiable ethical rule! [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h8)

question: Why is it important to include a data analysis plan in your research proposal?

options.A: To allow the hospital pharmacy to order more medication supplies
options.B: To calculate the exact travel expenses of the research team
options.C: To ensure that no patients ever experience physical pain
options.D: To prove that the collected data can actually answer the research questions

explanation: Showing your analysis plan ahead of time proves your study is well-thought-out and that your results will actually answer your research questions. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h8)

question: Which visual chart is most commonly used to map out a project timeline in a research proposal?

options.A: Scatter plot
options.B: Flowchart diagram
options.C: Gantt chart
options.D: Pie chart

explanation: A Gantt chart is a handy bar chart layout that helps you schedule out your project tasks and deadlines across the weeks or months of your study. [learn more](GNS224_U3_T2#GNS224_U3_T2_h9)

question: When it comes to formatting your paper, what golden rule connects your in-text citations and reference list?

options.A: Every in-text citation must match an entry in the reference list
